cards.title: Um planeta de água
cards.text: Os oceanos cobrem cerca de 71% da superfície da Terra e contêm 97% da sua água. Mesmo assim, mais de três quartos do fundo do mar ainda não foram mapeados em alta resolução.

deep.x: The ocean covers about 361 million km² and averages about 3,700 m deep. The Pacific alone is bigger than all Earth's land put together. Seen from space, Earth is unmistakably a blue planet.
Better maps of Mars?

Satellites measuring tiny bumps in the sea surface give us a rough map of the whole seafloor, with a resolution of a few kilometres. Detailed maps need ships with sonar. The international **Seabed 2030** project aims to map it all in high detail; by the mid-2020s only about a quarter was done.
The hidden landscape

The mid-ocean ridge system is the longest mountain range on Earth, winding round the globe like the seam on a tennis ball. Seamounts, undersea mountains, are hotspots for life, and many remain unvisited.
Unknown life
About 240,000 marine species have been described, but estimates suggest there could be one to two million or more. Expeditions regularly find dozens of new species in a single trip.
If Earth's surface were perfectly smooth, the ocean would cover it to a depth of about 2.7 km.
The ocean is Earth's largest habitat and its least explored, with most of its floor never seen in detail.

cards.title: As zonas do oceano
cards.text: A luz do sol diminui rápido com a profundidade. Abaixo de cerca de 200 m, há penumbra; abaixo de 1,000 m, escuridão total, onde muitos animais produzem a própria luz.

deep.x: Light fades rapidly with depth. Red light is absorbed in the first few metres, then orange and yellow, leaving only blue. That's why red animals in the deep look black, a perfect disguise.
The twilight zone

Not enough light reaches 200–1,000 m for photosynthesis, but enough for animals to see silhouettes against the faint glow above. Many fish here have huge upward-facing eyes. The **bristlemouth**, a fish the size of a finger, may be the most numerous vertebrate on Earth.
The biggest migration on Earth

Every night, billions of tonnes of small animals rise from the twilight zone to feed near the surface, then sink back before dawn to hide from predators. This **daily vertical migration** is so large it shows up on ships' sonar as a moving "false bottom".
Life in the dark
Deep-sea animals depend on **marine snow**: flakes of dead plankton, droppings and mucus drifting down from above. A flake may take weeks to reach the bottom.
The twilight zone may hold more fish by weight than the rest of the ocean combined, though estimates vary enormously.
The ocean is layered by light, and each layer has its own way of life.

cards.title: O ponto mais profundo
cards.text: O Challenger Deep, na Fossa das Marianas, tem cerca de 10,900 m de profundidade. O Monte Everest caberia lá dentro com mais de 2 km de sobra.

deep.x: The Mariana Trench curves for about 2,500 km through the western Pacific, near Guam. It's a **subduction zone**: the old, heavy Pacific plate dives beneath the smaller Mariana plate, dragging the seafloor down into a deep gash.

x: Challenger Deep ≈ 10,935 m
Everest ≈ 8,849 m
Everest's summit would sit about 2,100 m below the surface

deep.x: Who has been there

In 1960 Jacques Piccard and Don Walsh descended in the bathyscaphe *Trieste*. It took nearly five hours to go down; they stayed only 20 minutes and saw little through the stirred-up silt. Since 2019, a reusable submersible has carried dozens of people there.
Life at the bottom

Even at the bottom, there's life: shrimp-like amphipods, sea cucumbers and microbes. The deepest fish filmed, a snailfish, was seen at about 8,300 m in 2022. Fish probably can't live much deeper, because the chemistry that protects their proteins from pressure reaches its limit.

deep.w: Nothing lives at the very bottom of the ocean
deep.r: Amphipods, worms and microbes thrive even in the Challenger Deep

deep.x: The deepest ocean is deeper than the highest mountain is tall, and life still manages to live there.

cards.title: Pressão
cards.text: A pressão aumenta cerca de uma atmosfera a cada 10 metros. No fundo da Fossa das Marianas, ela é mais de 1,000 vezes a pressão da superfície.

deep.x: Air presses on you with a weight of about 1 atmosphere at sea level. Water is much denser, so every 10 m of seawater adds roughly another atmosphere. At 10 m you feel twice the surface pressure; at 100 m, eleven times.

x: Depth 10,900 m ÷ 10 m per atm ≈ 1,090 atm
+ 1 atm of air ≈ 1,091 atm
≈ 1.1 tonnes pressing on every square centimetre

deep.x: What happens to air

Gases squeeze. A balloon taken to 10 m shrinks to half its size; at 30 m, to a quarter. That's why scuba divers must rise slowly: gas dissolved in their blood under pressure can form bubbles if released too fast, causing **decompression sickness**.

v.unit: volume of a balloon of air, %

deep.x: How deep animals cope

Deep-sea animals have no air spaces to crush. Their bodies are mostly water, which barely compresses. Many fish carry a molecule called **TMAO** that stabilises proteins against pressure; it's also what gives fish their "fishy" smell when they decay.
Cuvier's beaked whales hold the record for deep-diving mammals: nearly 3,000 m, and one dive lasted almost 4 hours.
Water pressure grows by about one atmosphere every 10 m, so deep-sea life is built without air spaces to crush.

deep.w: Deep-sea fish explode when brought up
deep.r: They don't explode, but any gas inside expands and soft tissues sag, which is why they look so strange on deck

cards.title: Bioluminescência
cards.text: Cerca de três quartos dos animais do fundo do mar produzem luz, para atrair presas, encontrar parceiros ou confundir predadores. O peixe-pescador balança uma isca luminosa.

deep.x: Animals make light with a chemical reaction: an enzyme called **luciferase** helps a molecule called luciferin react with oxygen, releasing energy as light with very little heat. Some animals make the chemicals themselves; others, like the anglerfish, host glowing bacteria.
Why glow?

Hiding with light sounds odd, but it works. Seen from below, a fish's dark shape stands out against faint sunlight. Hatchetfish and some squid shine dim blue lights on their bellies to match the glow above, a trick called **counter-illumination**.
Mostly blue

Blue-green light travels farthest in seawater, so most deep-sea glow is blue, and most deep-sea animals can only see blue. A few dragonfish produce red light, invisible to their prey, like a secret searchlight.
On Portuguese beaches
On some summer nights, waves on Portuguese beaches sparkle blue. This is usually caused by dinoflagellates such as *Noctiluca*, single-celled plankton that flash when disturbed.
A glowing protein from a jellyfish, GFP, is now used in labs worldwide to tag cells and genes; its discoverers won the 2008 Nobel Prize in Chemistry.
In the dark ocean, light is a language: for hunting, hiding and finding a partner.

cards.title: Fitoplâncton
cards.text: Minúsculas plantas do oceano, chamadas fitoplâncton, produzem cerca de metade do oxigênio que respiramos e formam a base da teia alimentar marinha.

deep.x: Phytoplankton are microscopic algae and bacteria drifting in sunlit water. Most are far too small to see individually, but together they can colour the sea green, visible from space during spring blooms.
Small but mighty

Phytoplankton make up less than 1% of the weight of all photosynthesisers on Earth, yet do roughly half of all photosynthesis. The secret is speed: they can divide every day or so and are eaten almost as fast as they grow.
Feeding the ocean
The carbon pump

When phytoplankton die or are eaten, some of their carbon sinks to the deep sea in droppings and marine snow, where it can stay for centuries. This **biological pump** removes billions of tonnes of carbon from the surface each year.
The cyanobacterium *Prochlorococcus*, discovered only in the 1980s, is probably the most abundant photosynthetic organism on Earth.

deep.w: Rainforests make most of our oxygen
deep.r: Ocean phytoplankton produce about half, and forests use much of what they make

deep.x: The ocean's tiniest plants do about half the planet's photosynthesis.

cards.title: O oceano como depósito de calor
cards.text: O oceano absorveu mais de 90% do calor extra retido pelos gases de efeito estufa e cerca de um quarto das nossas emissões de CO₂, o que deixa a água do mar um pouco mais ácida.

deep.x: Water can store far more heat than air. The top few metres of the ocean hold as much heat as the entire atmosphere. Since the 1970s, the ocean has soaked up over 90% of the extra energy trapped by greenhouse gases, slowing the warming we feel on land.
The cost of a cooler sky

Warmer water expands. Together with melting ice, this has raised global sea level by about 20 cm since 1900, and the rate is now about 4 mm a year. Hotter seas also bring marine heatwaves that bleach corals and kill kelp forests.
Acidification
CO2 dissolving in seawater forms carbonic acid. Average surface pH has fallen from about 8.2 to 8.1. The sea is still alkaline, but less so.

x: pH is logarithmic
About 26–30% more hydrogen ions (acidity)

deep.x: Oysters, mussels, corals and tiny sea snails called pteropods need carbonate to build shells. Oyster hatcheries in the US Pacific Northwest have already had mass die-offs linked to acidic water.
The ocean's heat uptake is so large that if it all went into the lower atmosphere instead, air temperatures would have risen by tens of degrees.
The ocean has protected us from the worst of warming so far, but it's paying for it with heat and acid.

cards.title: Fontes hidrotermais
cards.text: No fundo do mar profundo, água quente e rica em minerais jorra de fontes. Ecossistemas inteiros vivem ali de energia química, sem luz do sol.

deep.x: In 1977 scientists in the submersible *Alvin* explored the Galápagos Rift, expecting bare rock. They found shimmering warm water and dense communities of giant tube worms, clams and crabs around it, 2,500 m down. It was one of biology's great surprises.
Life without sunlight

The base of these food webs is bacteria that get energy from chemicals, mainly hydrogen sulfide, a process called **chemosynthesis**. The water is far hotter than 100 °C but doesn't boil because of the enormous pressure.
Giant tube worms

*Riftia* tube worms grow up to about 2 m long and have no mouth or gut. Inside them live billions of bacteria that turn vent chemicals into food. The worm's red plume is coloured by haemoglobin, which carries oxygen and sulfide to its bacterial partners.
Vents near Portugal

These vent fields lie on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge within Portugal's waters. Black smokers there pour out metal-rich water, attracting interest in seabed mining; Portugal has backed a pause until the effects are better understood.
Some scientists think life on Earth may have begun at hydrothermal vents, where chemical energy and minerals were concentrated.
Hydrothermal vents showed that life doesn't need the Sun: chemical energy from Earth itself can feed whole ecosystems.

cards.title: Plástico no mar
cards.text: Milhões de toneladas de plástico entram no oceano todo ano. Ele se fragmenta em microplásticos, hoje encontrados da superfície até as fossas mais profundas.

deep.x: Estimates of how much plastic reaches the ocean each year vary from around 1 to over 10 million tonnes. It comes from rivers, beaches, fishing and wastewater. Only about 9% of all plastic ever made has been recycled.
Where it ends up

The Great Pacific Garbage Patch, a zone where currents gather floating debris, covers about 1.6 million km². It isn't a solid island but a thin soup of fragments; by weight, almost half is lost or dumped fishing gear.
Breaking down, not away

Sunlight and waves break plastic into ever smaller pieces. Pieces under 5 mm are called **microplastics**. They've been found in Arctic ice, deep-sea sediments, Mariana Trench animals, seafood, table salt and human blood.
Harm to wildlife
What's being done

Portugal introduced a charge on light plastic bags in 2015, and their use dropped sharply. The EU banned many single-use plastics, such as cutlery, straws and plates, from 2021. Negotiations on a global plastics treaty began in 2022 but have struggled to reach agreement.

deep.w: Recycling will solve the problem
deep.r: Most plastic isn't recycled; cutting use and stopping leaks matter most

deep.x: Plastic doesn't disappear in the sea; it just gets smaller and spreads further.

cards.title: O oceano de Portugal
cards.text: As águas de Portugal, incluindo os Açores e a Madeira, formam uma das maiores zonas econômicas exclusivas da Europa, cerca de 18 vezes a sua área terrestre.

deep.x: An **exclusive economic zone** (EEZ) is the sea up to 200 nautical miles (about 370 km) from a country's coast, where it controls fishing, energy and mining. Because the Azores and Madeira are scattered far into the Atlantic, Portugal's EEZ is huge.

x: Total EEZ ≈ 1.7 million km²
Land ≈ 92,000 km²
Ratio ≈ 18–19 times

deep.x: Portugal has also asked the UN to extend its rights over the seabed on its continental shelf. If approved, its seabed area would be roughly 40 times its land area.
A rich sea

The Nazaré Canyon, up to about 5,000 m deep, funnels Atlantic swell towards the coast and builds some of the biggest surfable waves on Earth. Off the Azores, former whaling boats now take tourists whale-watching; commercial whaling there ended in 1987.
Eating the sea
Portuguese people eat about 55–60 kg of fish and seafood per person per year, the highest in the EU and among the highest in the world.
Protecting it
In 2024 the Azores approved the largest marine protected area network in the North Atlantic, covering about 30% of its waters, half of that fully protected from fishing.
A surfer rode a wave at Nazaré in 2020 measured at about 26 m, recognised as the largest wave ever surfed.
Portugal is a small country on land but a maritime giant, with an ocean territory many times larger than its soil.

cards.title: A era dos dinossauros
cards.text: Os dinossauros surgiram há cerca de 230 milhões de anos e dominaram a terra firme por mais de 160 milhões de anos, nos períodos Triássico, Jurássico e Cretáceo.

deep.x: Geologists call the age of dinosaurs the **Mesozoic** era, which ran from about 252 to 66 million years ago. It began after the worst mass extinction in Earth's history and ended with an asteroid.
A slow start

The earliest known dinosaurs, such as Eoraptor and Herrerasaurus from Argentina, were small to medium two-legged animals. For their first 30 million years they shared the land with crocodile relatives that were often bigger and more common. A mass extinction about 201 million years ago wiped out many of those rivals, and dinosaurs took over.
The end

About 66 million years ago an asteroid roughly 10 km wide hit what is now Mexico's Yucatán Peninsula, leaving the Chicxulub crater, about 180 km across. Dust and soot blocked sunlight, food chains collapsed, and all dinosaurs died out except the birds.

x: Non-bird dinosaurs existed ≈ 165 million years
Homo sapiens so far ≈ 0.3 million years
Dinosaurs lasted about 550 times longer

deep.x: During the Mesozoic the supercontinent Pangaea split apart and the Atlantic Ocean opened, slowly separating Portugal from North America.
Dinosaurs ruled for over 160 million years; our species has been around for about 0.3 million.

cards.title: T. rex e estegossauro
cards.text: O estegossauro viveu há cerca de 150 milhões de anos; o T. rex, há cerca de 68–66 milhões. O T. rex viveu mais perto de nós no tempo do que do estegossauro.

deep.x: "Prehistoric" squashes a vast span of time into one word. Stegosaurus lived in the Late Jurassic, about 155 to 150 million years ago. Tyrannosaurus rex lived at the very end of the Cretaceous, about 68 to 66 million years ago.

x: Stegosaurus ≈ 150 Ma, T. rex ≈ 67 Ma
Gap between them ≈ 83 million years
T. rex to us ≈ 66 million years

deep.x: Different worlds

In Stegosaurus's time there were no flowering plants; the landscape was ferns, cycads and conifers. By T. rex's time flowers, and many modern insects that pollinate them, had spread across the land. Stegosaurus's predator was Allosaurus, not T. rex.
Getting a feel for it

A similar trick works with human history. Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza. Deep time is so long that even "ancient" things are spread far apart.
Stegosaurus fossils have also been found in Portugal, in the Late Jurassic rocks around Lourinhã.

deep.w: All dinosaurs lived together
deep.r: Different dinosaurs were separated by tens of millions of years

deep.x: T. rex is closer in time to your smartphone than to Stegosaurus.

cards.title: As aves são dinossauros
cards.text: As aves evoluíram de pequenos dinossauros terópodes com penas. Um pardal é, tecnicamente, um dinossauro vivo, mais aparentado com o T. rex do que o T. rex era com o estegossauro.

deep.x: Scientists classify animals by shared ancestry, like a family tree. Birds sit inside the dinosaur tree, on the branch of **theropods**, the mostly meat-eating two-legged dinosaurs that also include T. rex and Velociraptor.
The evidence

In 1861, just two years after Darwin's Origin of Species, quarry workers in Germany found **Archaeopteryx**, about 150 million years old, with feathered wings but also teeth, claws and a bony tail. In the 1960s the American palaeontologist John Ostrom noticed how much the small predator Deinonychus resembled birds. Since the 1990s, feathered dinosaur fossils from China have settled the question.
Who's related to whom
T. rex and a sparrow share a common ancestor within the theropods. To find the ancestor T. rex shares with Stegosaurus, you have to go back to the very base of the dinosaur family tree.
There are about 11,000 species of birds today, nearly twice as many as there are species of mammals, so dinosaurs are arguably still thriving.
Dinosaurs didn't all die out: about 11,000 species of them are flying around today.

cards.title: Penas
cards.text: Muitos dinossauros tinham penas ou penugem. Fósseis da China mostram padrões de cor preservados em estruturas de pigmento.

deep.x: In 1996 Chinese scientists described **Sinosauropteryx**, a small predator from Liaoning province covered in simple fuzzy filaments. It was the first non-bird dinosaur found with feathers. Since then dozens of feathered species have turned up.
Colours from fossils

Feathers contain tiny pigment packets called **melanosomes**. Their shape reveals their colour: sausage shapes for black and grey, rounder ones for reddish brown. In 2010 scientists used this to show Sinosauropteryx had a ginger-and-white striped tail and Anchiornis had black-and-white wings with a reddish crest.
Feathers came before flight

Early feathers were for warmth and display, not flight. Yutyrannus, a 9 m relative of T. rex described in 2012, was covered in long filaments. Some plant-eating dinosaurs also had fuzz, so feathers may go back to the earliest dinosaurs.

deep.w: T. rex was covered in feathers
deep.r: Its relatives had feathers, but skin impressions suggest adult T. rex was mostly scaly

deep.x: Microraptor, a crow-sized dinosaur with four feathered wings, had glossy black iridescent feathers like a modern starling.
Many dinosaurs were fluffy and colourful, and feathers evolved for warmth and show long before flight.

cards.title: Gigantes
cards.text: Saurópodes como o Argentinosaurus podem ter chegado a cerca de 35 m e 70 toneladas, os maiores animais terrestres de todos os tempos. Ossos ocos os ajudavam a sustentar o seu tamanho.

deep.x: **Sauropods** were long-necked plant-eaters with small heads, pillar-like legs and long tails. They include Brachiosaurus, Diplodocus and the true giants of the Cretaceous, the titanosaurs.
How big, really?

Argentinosaurus lived about 95 million years ago in what is now Argentina. It is known from only a few bones, including huge vertebrae, so its size is estimated by comparison with better-known relatives. Estimates run from about 30 to 35 m long and 60 to 75 tonnes. The blue whale is heavier, but water supports its weight.
How they managed
Sauropods had a bird-like breathing system with air sacs that reached into their bones, making their skeletons lighter. By not chewing, they could keep their heads small and their necks long.
Small eggs, fast growth
Their eggs were only about the size of a football. Babies grew enormously fast, gaining perhaps several kilograms a day at their peak.
Portugal had its own sauropod, Lusotitan, a Brachiosaurus relative from the Late Jurassic rocks around Lourinhã.
Air-filled bones and bird-like breathing let sauropods become the largest animals ever to walk on land.

cards.title: Não são dinossauros
cards.text: Os pterossauros (répteis voadores) e os répteis marinhos, como os plesiossauros, viveram ao lado dos dinossauros, mas não eram dinossauros.

deep.x: "Dinosaur" has a precise scientific meaning. Dinosaurs share features of the hips and legs: their legs were held straight under the body, like a horse, not sprawled out sideways like a lizard. The hip socket has a hole right through it.
Pterosaurs

Pterosaurs were the first vertebrates to fly with flapping wings, about 80 million years before birds. Their wings were skin membranes stretched from a hugely long fourth finger. Quetzalcoatlus had a wingspan of about 10 to 11 m, like a small plane. They were close cousins of dinosaurs but on a separate branch.
Sea monsters

Marine reptiles evolved from land reptiles that returned to the sea. Mosasaurs are actually lizards, related to monitor lizards and snakes. Many of the first ichthyosaur and plesiosaur skeletons were found in the early 1800s by the English fossil hunter Mary Anning.

deep.w: Dimetrodon, the sail-backed beast, was a dinosaur
deep.r: It lived 40 million years before them and is closer to mammals

deep.x: Pterosaurs ruled the air and marine reptiles the sea, but only land animals with upright legs were dinosaurs.

cards.title: Os dinossauros de Portugal
cards.text: A Lourinhã, ao norte de Lisboa, é um dos sítios de dinossauros mais ricos da Europa. O Lourinhanosaurus recebeu o nome dela, e lá foram encontrados ovos fósseis de dinossauro com embriões.

deep.x: About 150 million years ago, the Atlantic was a narrow sea and Iberia sat close to North America. The rivers and floodplains of the time left thick layers of rock around Lourinhã, now called the **Lourinhã Formation**. Its animals look a lot like those of the famous Morrison Formation in the USA.
Eggs with embryos

In 1993 Isabel Mateus and her family found a clutch of over 100 dinosaur eggs at Paimogo beach near Lourinhã. Some contained tiny embryonic bones, among the oldest dinosaur embryos known. They were identified as Lourinhanosaurus, named in 1998.
Footprints across the country

x: Pedreira do Galinha, in the Serra de Aire: some of the oldest and longest sauropod trackways known, about 175 million years old
Cabo Espichel: dinosaur tracks on steep cliffs, linked to a local legend of a giant mule
Carenque, near Lisbon: a Cretaceous trackway preserved beside a motorway tunnel

deep.x: Torvosaurus gurneyi, found in Portugal, is the largest land predator yet known from Europe.
Portugal's Jurassic rocks hold eggs, embryos, giants and trackways that make it one of Europe's best dinosaur regions.

cards.title: Como se formam os fósseis
cards.text: Um animal é soterrado rapidamente por sedimentos; com o tempo, minerais substituem seus ossos e os transformam em pedra. Só uma fração minúscula dos seres vivos chega a fossilizar.

deep.x: Most dead animals are eaten, rot or are scattered within weeks. To become a fossil, a body usually needs to be buried quickly, out of reach of scavengers and oxygen.
Turning to stone

Groundwater carrying dissolved minerals such as silica or calcite seeps through buried bone. The minerals fill the tiny spaces and can gradually replace the original material. The bone keeps its shape but becomes rock, a process called **permineralisation**.
Kinds of fossil
Why so few

Hard parts fossilise far better than soft ones, and lakes, rivers and seabeds are better than forests or mountains. Then the rock has to survive millions of years of heat and pressure, be lifted to the surface, and be found before it erodes away. Only a tiny fraction of all animals that ever lived became fossils, and an even tinier fraction have been found.
Rare sites with exceptional preservation, such as the Solnhofen limestone in Germany or volcanic ash beds in China, keep feathers and even skin.

deep.w: Fossils are the original bones
deep.r: Most dinosaur fossils are rock that has copied the bone's shape

deep.x: A fossil is usually a rock copy of a body that was buried fast and lucky enough to survive.

cards.title: Datar fósseis
cards.text: Os fósseis são datados pelas camadas de rocha ao seu redor. As camadas vulcânicas podem ser datadas com precisão usando elementos radioativos que decaem a ritmos conhecidos.

deep.x: There are two kinds of dating. **Relative dating** puts rocks in order: in undisturbed layers, the lower ones are older. The Danish scientist Nicolas Steno set out this principle in 1669. **Absolute dating** gives an age in years.
Radioactive clocks

Some elements in volcanic rock are radioactive and decay at a fixed rate. Each has a **half-life**, the time for half of it to decay. By measuring how much has turned into its "daughter" element, scientists work out when the rock cooled.

x: Uranium-238 half-life ≈ 4.5 billion years
Rock with 1% decayed
Age ≈ 65 million years

deep.x: The sandwich

Fossils themselves rarely contain the right minerals. So scientists date volcanic ash layers above and below, and the fossil must lie between those ages. **Index fossils**, such as ammonites that lived for short, known periods, help match layers between distant sites.

deep.w: Dinosaurs are carbon dated
deep.r: Carbon-14 is useless beyond about 50,000 years; dinosaurs need uranium or argon

deep.x: Rock layers give the order; radioactive clocks in volcanic ash give the dates.

cards.title: A descoberta dos dinossauros
cards.text: A palavra "dinossauro", que significa "lagarto terrível", foi criada por Richard Owen em 1842. Novas espécies ainda são batizadas a um ritmo de cerca de 50 por ano.

deep.x: People found dinosaur bones for centuries without knowing what they were; some were taken for giants or dragons. Scientific study began in England in the 1820s.
Naming the group

The anatomist Richard Owen noticed that Megalosaurus, Iguanodon and Hylaeosaurus shared features no living reptile had. In 1842 he grouped them as **Dinosauria**, from Greek deinos, "terribly great", and sauros, "lizard". Owen meant "awe-inspiringly big" as much as "terrible".
The Bone Wars

In the late 1800s two American palaeontologists, Othniel Marsh and Edward Cope, raced to find new species in the American West. Their bitter rivalry included bribery and smashing fossils to keep them from each other. Together they named well over 100 species, including Stegosaurus and Triceratops.
Still discovering

Today about 50 new species are named each year, many from China, Argentina and the USA. The total is now well over 1,000. Better imaging, such as CT scans, also reveals details like brain shape and inner ear inside old fossils.
Many experts think we know only a small share of the dinosaur species that ever lived.
We are living through a golden age of dinosaur discovery, with about one new species a week.

quiz.q: Qual viveu mais perto, no tempo, dos humanos do que do estegossauro?
quiz.explain: Cerca de 80 milhões de anos separam o T. rex do estegossauro.

quiz.explain: As aves evoluíram de dinossauros com penas.

cards.title: Feitas para voar
cards.text: As aves têm ossos ocos, músculos peitorais potentes e um sistema respiratório de fluxo único supereficiente. Algumas conseguem voar por cima do Himalaia.

deep.x: Flight is the most energy-hungry way to move. Almost everything about a bird's body is shaped by two needs: keep weight down and deliver huge amounts of power.
Muscle power

The main flight muscles can make up around a quarter of a flying bird's body mass. They attach to a deep ridge on the breastbone called the **keel**. The downstroke muscle is the breast meat you eat on a chicken.
One-way breathing

Birds have about nine air sacs that act as bellows, pushing air through the lungs in one direction during both breathing in and breathing out. That lets them extract oxygen where mammals would struggle.
High flyers
Bar-headed geese migrate across the Himalayas, reaching altitudes of over 6,000 m. In 1973 a Rüppell's vulture collided with a plane over Ivory Coast at about 11,300 m.

deep.w: Bird skeletons are unusually light
deep.r: They weigh about the same share of body mass as a mammal's; the bones are hollow but denser

deep.x: Birds fly on hollow, strutted bones, a keel of muscle and lungs that breathe in one direction.

cards.title: Penas
cards.text: As penas são feitas de queratina, como as suas unhas. Tipos diferentes isolam do frio, impermeabilizam, exibem cores ou dão sustentação no voo.

deep.x: Feathers are the one feature only birds have today. They are made of **keratin**, the protein family in your nails and hair, though birds use a different, stiffer type.
How a feather is built

A central shaft, the **rachis**, carries rows of branches called barbs. Each barb has smaller barbules with tiny hooks that lock onto their neighbours like Velcro. When a feather splits, preening zips it back together.
Different jobs
Waterbirds spread oil from a gland near the tail to keep feathers waterproof. Feathers wear out, so most birds replace them at least once a year in a **moult**.
Colour tricks

Some colours are pigments, like the pink of flamingos, which comes from carotenoids in their food. Others are structural: the blue of a jay or kingfisher comes from microscopic structures that scatter light. Grind a blue feather and the blue disappears.
A ruby-throated hummingbird has about 1,000 feathers; a swan can have about 25,000.
Feathers are keratin built like a zip, specialised for flight, warmth, waterproofing and show.

cards.title: A inteligência das aves
cards.text: Corvos e papagaios resolvem quebra-cabeças, usam ferramentas e se lembram de rostos. Os corvos-da-nova-caledônia fabricam ganchos com gravetos.

deep.x: "Bird brain" used to be an insult. Bird brains are small, but in parrots and songbirds the neurons are packed very densely. A 2016 study found some parrots and crows have as many neurons in their forebrain as some monkeys.
Tools and planning

In 2002 a captive New Caledonian crow called Betty, at Oxford, bent a straight piece of wire into a hook to lift a food bucket from a tube. Wild crows of the same species make hooked tools from twigs and leaves and keep them for later use.
Remembering faces

In Seattle, researchers trapped crows while wearing a particular mask. For years afterwards, crows scolded anyone wearing that mask, including birds that had never been caught. They had learned from the others.
A different design
Bird brains are organised differently from ours, with nerve cells in clusters rather than layers. Similar intelligence evolved twice, in mammals and in birds, from different wiring.

deep.w: Small brain means low intelligence
deep.r: Corvid and parrot brains pack neurons densely and rival apes on some tasks

deep.x: Crows and parrots pack primate-like numbers of neurons into small brains, and use them to plan, make tools and remember.

cards.title: O canto das aves
cards.text: As aves canoras aprendem o canto com os adultos, mais ou menos como as crianças aprendem a falar, e muitas têm dialetos regionais.

deep.x: About half of all bird species are **songbirds**, which learn their songs. Parrots and hummingbirds learn sounds too. Among mammals, vocal learning is rare: humans, whales, dolphins, some bats and elephants.
Like learning to talk

A young songbird has a sensitive period for listening, much as children absorb language easily when young. It then practises with quiet, rambling **subsong**, like a baby's babbling, gradually refining it. A bird raised without hearing an adult sings an abnormal song. A gene called FOXP2 is involved in vocal learning in both birds and people.
Dialects

Because songs are copied, they drift from place to place. In the 1960s, the American biologist Peter Marler showed that white-crowned sparrows around San Francisco Bay had distinct local dialects. Chaffinches in Europe also have regional variations.
Two voices
Birds sing with a **syrinx**, an organ where the windpipe splits into two. Each side can work separately, so some birds sing two notes at once.
In temperate regions mostly males sing, but in many tropical species females sing too, and some pairs sing duets.
Songbirds learn their songs from adults during a sensitive period, so local dialects spread like accents.

cards.title: Migração
cards.text: Todo outono, bilhões de aves migram. Elas se orientam pelo Sol, pelas estrelas, pelo campo magnético da Terra e por pontos de referência.

deep.x: An estimated 2 billion small birds fly from Europe to Africa each autumn. They follow seasonal food: insects vanish in a European winter but are plentiful south of the Sahara.
Record breakers

In 2022 a young bar-tailed godwit flew about 13,500 km nonstop from Alaska to Tasmania in 11 days. Arctic terns travel from the Arctic to Antarctica and back each year, about 70,000 km on a wandering route.
The navigation toolkit

In the 1960s Stephen Emlen raised indigo buntings in a planetarium and showed they learn north by watching which point the night sky rotates around. Birds may sense Earth's magnetic field using a protein called cryptochrome in their eyes, though how exactly is still debated.
Portugal on the flyway
Portugal sits on a major route. In autumn, Sagres and Cabo de São Vicente see thousands of raptors and storks heading south, and the Tagus estuary hosts tens of thousands of wintering wading birds.
Caged migratory birds become restless at night during migration season, fluttering in the direction they would fly. Scientists call it Zugunruhe, "migration restlessness".
Migrating birds combine a sun clock, star map, magnetic sense and memory to cross continents.

cards.title: As cegonhas em Portugal

items: migram para a África todo inverno
muitas ficam o ano todo na Ibéria

cards.text: Antigamente, todas as cegonhas-brancas migravam para a África; hoje, muitas ficam o ano todo em Portugal, comendo em aterros e arrozais. Seus ninhos coroam igrejas e torres de alta tensão.

deep.x: The white stork is one of Portugal's most visible birds: tall, white with black wing feathers, a red bill and red legs. Storks are almost silent; instead of singing they clatter their bills loudly at the nest.
A changing migration

Traditionally, nearly all European white storks flew to Africa south of the Sahara for the winter, soaring on rising warm air over the Strait of Gibraltar. Since the 1980s, more and more stay in Iberia all year.
Why they stay

x: Open landfill sites provide food all year; GPS-tracked storks in Portugal visit them daily
Rice fields host the invasive red swamp crayfish, an easy meal
Milder winters make staying less risky

deep.x: Portugal's breeding population has grown many times over since the 1980s, to over 10,000 pairs. EU rules phasing out open landfills could change their habits again.
Nests on high

Stork nests are huge piles of sticks reused and enlarged each year, sometimes over a metre wide. They crown church towers, chimneys and electricity pylons, where power companies often fit platforms to keep nests away from live wires.
The legend of storks delivering babies comes from northern European folklore, where storks returning in spring were seen as bringers of new life.
Portugal's storks increasingly skip Africa, staying all year thanks to landfills, rice fields and milder winters.

cards.title: A mais rápida e a maior
cards.text: O avestruz é a maior ave, com até 2,7 m de altura, e corre a cerca de 70 km/h. O colibri-abelha, com uns 5 cm, é a menor.

deep.x: Birds range from a bee-sized hummingbird to flightless giants, and from slow fliers to the fastest animal on Earth.
The ostrich

Male ostriches can weigh around 150 kg. Their long legs have only two toes, and they can sprint at about 70 km/h and keep up 50 km/h for long distances. An ostrich egg weighs about 1.4 kg, about as much as two dozen hen's eggs.
The bee hummingbird
Found only in Cuba, the bee hummingbird is about 5 to 6 cm long and weighs about 2 g, less than a 1-cent euro coin (2.3 g). Its nest is the size of a small cup.
The fastest
The peregrine falcon dives on prey at over 300 km/h, the fastest speed of any animal. Peregrines breed on cliffs along the Portuguese coast and sometimes on city buildings.
Common swifts, which nest in Lisbon's old buildings each summer, can stay airborne for about 10 months without landing, even sleeping on the wing.
Birds span from a 2 g hummingbird to a 150 kg ostrich, and include the fastest animal alive.

cards.title: Beija-flores
cards.text: Os beija-flores batem as asas até 80 vezes por segundo e conseguem voar para trás. O coração deles pode bater mais de 1,000 vezes por minuto.

deep.x: There are about 360 species of hummingbird, all living in the Americas. They are built for hovering in front of flowers to drink nectar.
How they hover

Most birds get lift only on the downstroke. Hummingbirds rotate their wings at the shoulder, tracing a figure of eight, so they get lift on the upstroke too, about a quarter of the total. That lets them hover, and fly sideways and backwards.
Living fast

Hummingbirds have the highest metabolism of any warm-blooded animal relative to size. They feed every few minutes during the day. At night many go into **torpor**: body temperature drops steeply and metabolism falls by up to about 95%, saving energy until morning.
A European past
Fossils about 30 million years old found in Germany show that birds very close to modern hummingbirds once lived in Europe. Later they disappeared from the Old World.
The ruby-throated hummingbird, weighing about 3 g, crosses the Gulf of Mexico nonstop, about 800 km, on its migration.
Hummingbirds hover by getting lift on both wing strokes, powered by the fastest metabolism of any bird.

cards.title: Pinguins

items.l: machos em jejum sobre o ovo

cards.text: Os pinguins "voam" debaixo d'água. Os pinguins-imperadores mergulham a mais de 500 m, e os machos chocam o ovo sobre os pés durante o inverno antártico, sem comer.

deep.x: There are 18 species of penguin, all in the Southern Hemisphere. The Galápagos penguin is the only one that reaches just north of the equator.
Flying underwater
Penguins' wings became stiff flippers. Unlike flying birds, they have solid, heavy bones, which help them dive. Dark backs and white bellies hide them from predators above and below.
The emperor's winter

Emperor penguins breed on sea ice in the Antarctic winter. After the female lays a single egg, she passes it to the male and heads to sea to feed. He balances it on his feet under a fold of skin for about two months, in temperatures that can fall below −40 °C with wind chill. Thousands of males huddle, slowly rotating so each takes a turn on the cold outside.

x: Male fasts about 4 months
Starts at about 38 kg
Can lose up to about 40% of his body weight

deep.x: A warming threat
Emperors need stable sea ice from April to December. Recent years of record-low Antarctic sea ice have caused colonies to fail, and scientists warn many could vanish by 2100.
If the female is late, the male can feed the newly hatched chick a protein-rich secretion from his oesophagus.
Penguins traded flight in air for flight in water, and emperors raise chicks through the harshest winter on Earth.

cards.title: Começar a observar aves
cards.text: Comece com um comedouro ou um parque. Repare no tamanho, na cor, no formato do bico e no comportamento. Um app gratuito consegue identificar aves por fotos ou pelo canto.

deep.x: Birdwatching needs little equipment and works anywhere, from a balcony in Porto to a beach in the Algarve. The key is learning to look systematically.
What to notice
Beak shape is a great clue: thick and conical for seeds, like a finch; thin and pointed for insects, like a robin; hooked for meat, like a kestrel.
Gear
Binoculars are labelled with two numbers, such as 8×42. The first is magnification, the second the width of the front lenses in millimetres; wider lenses let in more light.

x: 8 = makes birds look 8 times closer
42 = 42 mm lenses, bright in dim light

deep.x: Apps that help
Where to start in Portugal

Common garden birds include the house sparrow, blackbird, great tit, robin, serin and white wagtail. For more, try the Tagus estuary for flamingos, Ria Formosa in the Algarve for wading birds, or Castro Verde for steppe birds like the great bustard. SPEA, the Portuguese bird society, runs guided walks and bird counts.
Recording sightings in apps like eBird helps scientists track bird populations and migration across Europe.
Notice size, shape, beak and behaviour first; apps and binoculars do the rest.

lessons.title: Insetos
lessons.summary: Os animais mais bem-sucedidos da Terra.

cards.title: Insetos em números
cards.text: Cerca de um milhão de espécies de insetos já foram descritas, e pode haver vários milhões a mais. A qualquer momento, talvez 10 quintilhões de insetos estejam vivos.

deep.x: Scientists have named about a million insect species, more than all other animals put together. Most estimates of the true total land around 5 million, though some go far higher. Every year roughly 10,000 new insect species are described, many from tropical forests where few people have looked.
Beetles lead the way

About 400,000 beetle species are known, roughly a quarter of all described animals. A famous quip, attributed to the biologist J. B. S. Haldane, says the creator must have had "an inordinate fondness for beetles".
Why so many?

x: Small size: one tree can host hundreds of species, each using a different part
Wings: insects were the first animals to fly, over 300 million years ago
Fast generations: some breed many times a year, so evolution moves quickly
Metamorphosis: young and adults eat different food and don't compete
About 10 quintillion insects alive
About 8 billion people
Over 1 billion insects per person

deep.x: Insects have survived all five mass extinctions, including the asteroid that ended the dinosaurs 66 million years ago.
By species count, Earth is a planet of insects, and beetles above all.

cards.title: O plano do corpo
cards.text: Todos os insetos têm seis pernas, três partes do corpo (cabeça, tórax e abdome) e geralmente dois pares de asas. As aranhas, com oito pernas, não são insetos.

deep.x: Every insect is built on the same pattern. The **head** carries the eyes, a pair of antennae and the mouthparts. The **thorax** is the engine room, holding all six legs and the wings. The **abdomen** contains most of the gut, the heart and the reproductive organs.
Armour on the outside

Insects have no internal skeleton. Instead they wear an **exoskeleton** made largely of chitin, a tough material that protects them and stops them drying out. Because it can't stretch, a growing insect must moult: it splits its old skin and pumps itself up before the new one hardens.
Breathing through holes

Insects have no lungs. Air enters through small holes along the sides called spiracles, then travels down branching tubes straight to the tissues. This system works well over short distances, one reason insects stay small today. About 300 million years ago, when the air held more oxygen, dragonfly-like insects reached wingspans of around 70 cm.

x: Flies have only one pair of wings; the second pair became tiny balancing knobs
Beetles' front wings became hard cases that protect the flying wings beneath
Fleas, lice and silverfish have no wings at all

deep.w: Spiders, woodlice and centipedes are insects
deep.r: They are arthropods, cousins of insects; insects are only those with six legs and three body parts

deep.x: Count the legs: six legs on a three-part body means an insect.

cards.title: Metamorfose
cards.text: As borboletas se transformam por completo: ovo, lagarta, crisálida, adulto. Dentro da crisálida, o corpo da lagarta se dissolve em grande parte e se reconstrói.

deep.x: Most insect species go through **complete metamorphosis**: egg, larva, pupa, adult. Beetles, flies, bees, ants, butterflies and moths all do it. The larva is an eating machine; a caterpillar can end up thousands of times heavier than when it hatched.
Soup, but not quite

Inside the chrysalis, digestive enzymes break down much of the caterpillar's tissue. But some parts survive. Small clusters of cells called **imaginal discs** have waited, dormant, since the egg. They now use the soup as raw material to build wings, legs, antennae and adult eyes. Hormones decide the timing: when a hormone that keeps the insect "young" drops, the next moult becomes the change into a pupa.
The other way to grow up
Grasshoppers, dragonflies, cockroaches and bugs use **incomplete metamorphosis**. Their young, called nymphs, look like small wingless adults and grow through a series of moults.

Complete metamorphosis has a big advantage: larvae and adults live different lives and don't compete for food. It may help explain why the groups that use it make up the large majority of insect species.
In a 2008 experiment, caterpillars trained to avoid a smell still avoided it as adult moths, so some memory survives the rebuild.
A chrysalis isn't resting: it's a construction site that turns an eating body into a flying, breeding one.

cards.title: Polinizadores
cards.text: Cerca de três quartos das principais culturas alimentares se beneficiam de animais polinizadores, sobretudo insetos. Sem eles, haveria muito menos frutas, castanhas e legumes.

deep.x: Many plants can't move their pollen themselves, so they pay animals to do it with nectar and spare pollen. A 2007 global study found that about three-quarters of leading food crops benefit from animal pollination. Insects do most of this work: bees above all, but also hoverflies, butterflies, moths, beetles and wasps.
Which foods depend on it?
The world's staple grains, such as wheat, rice and maize, are pollinated by the wind. So pollinators supply a smaller share of our calories, but a large share of our vitamins and variety.
Wild bees matter too

Honeybees get the attention, but Europe has about 2,000 species of wild bee. Many are better at certain crops. Bumblebees, for example, shake tomato flowers with a fast buzz that releases pollen honeybees can't reach.
What it's worth

In the EU, about €15 billion of farm output a year is linked directly to insect pollinators. In Portugal, apples from Alcobaça, cherries from Fundão and the fast-growing almond orchards of the Alentejo all rely on them.

deep.w: Honeybees do all the pollinating
deep.r: Wild bees, hoverflies and other insects do much of it, and some crops depend on them

deep.x: Pollinators don't feed us bread, but they give us most of our colour and flavour.

cards.title: Abelhas

items.b: todas fêmeas, fazem todo o resto

cards.text: Uma colmeia de abelhas tem uma rainha, milhares de operárias e alguns zangões. As tarefas das operárias mudam com a idade, da limpeza à coleta de alimento.

deep.x: A honeybee colony is a family. In summer it may hold 20,000 to 60,000 workers, all daughters of one queen. The queen can lay up to about 2,000 eggs a day. Drones are males; their only role is to mate with a queen from another colony, and they are pushed out in autumn.
A career that changes with age
A worker's job depends on how old she is, as her glands develop and then change:
Summer workers live only about five to six weeks; the last weeks are spent flying. Bees born in autumn can live for months, keeping the queen warm through winter.
Queen or worker?
Queens and workers come from the same kind of egg. The difference is food: a larva fed lots of **royal jelly** becomes a queen. Drones grow from unfertilised eggs.
The waggle dance

A forager who finds good flowers returns and dances. The angle of her waggle run shows the direction relative to the Sun; its length shows the distance. Karl von Frisch decoded this and shared the 1973 Nobel Prize.

x: One forager makes about 1/12 teaspoon of honey in her life, roughly 0.6 g
A 500 g jar ÷ 0.6 g
The lifetime work of about 800 bees

deep.x: The Asian hornet, which hunts honeybees, was first detected in Portugal around Viana do Castelo in 2011 and has since spread across much of the country.
A colony works like one big body, and each bee's job is set by her age.

cards.title: Formigas
cards.text: As formigas criam pulgões para obter melada, cultivam jardins de fungos e constroem pontes vivas com o próprio corpo. Sua massa total pode rivalizar com a de todas as aves e mamíferos selvagens juntos.

deep.x: About 14,000 ant species are known. All live in colonies, from a few dozen workers to many millions. Like bees, most workers are sterile females, and like bees they evolved from wasp ancestors.
Farmers and builders

Leafcutter ants of the Americas don't eat the leaves they carry. They chew them into a compost that feeds a fungus, and the fungus feeds the colony. They began farming about 50 million years ago, long before humans did.
How many ants?

A 2022 study estimated about 20 quadrillion ants on Earth. Their combined dry carbon mass, about 12 million tonnes, is more than all wild birds and wild mammals combined, and about a fifth of the mass of all humans.

x: About 20 quadrillion ants
About 8 billion people
About 2.5 million ants per person

deep.x: A supercolony in Europe
The Argentine ant, brought by human trade, forms a single giant colony along about 6,000 km of southern Europe's coast, from Italy to Portugal. Ants from distant nests treat each other as nestmates.

deep.w: Ants are led by a queen giving orders
deep.r: The queen only lays eggs; work is organised by simple rules and chemical signals between workers

deep.x: No ant is in charge, yet millions together farm, build and fight like one organism.

cards.title: Os sentidos dos insetos
cards.text: As abelhas veem nas flores padrões ultravioleta invisíveis para nós. As mariposas sentem o cheiro de parceiros a quilômetros de distância. Os olhos das moscas processam o movimento várias vezes mais rápido que os nossos.

deep.x: Insects live in a sensory world very different from ours. A honeybee's eyes are tuned to ultraviolet, blue and green. She can't see red, but she sees ultraviolet "landing strips" on many flowers that guide her to the nectar.
Smell at a distance

Male moths have feathery antennae covered in thousands of sensors. In some species they can find a female from several kilometres away, following a few molecules of her scent. The first such sex scent, or **pheromone**, was identified in silk moths in 1959.
Fast eyes

An insect's **compound eye** is made of many small units, each pointing in a slightly different direction. A dragonfly has up to about 30,000. Flies' eyes refresh much faster than ours, so to a fly a swatting hand looks slow.

v.unit: flashes per second seen as separate

deep.x: Senses in odd places

x: Butterflies and flies taste with their feet
Crickets hear through ears on their front legs
Mosquitoes track the carbon dioxide in your breath from tens of metres

deep.x: Because they see ultraviolet, bees see sunflowers with a dark bullseye in the middle, invisible to us.
Insects don't see a dimmer version of our world; they sense a different one.

cards.title: O declínio dos insetos
cards.text: Estudos em muitas regiões mostram quedas no número de insetos, causadas pela perda de habitat, pelos pesticidas, pela poluição luminosa e pelas mudanças climáticas.

deep.x: In 2017 a team studying nature reserves in Germany reported that the weight of flying insects caught in traps had fallen by more than 75% in 27 years. The study made headlines and triggered many more.
A mixed but worrying picture

A 2020 review of many long-term studies found land insects declining by roughly 9% per decade on average, though with large differences between places. Some freshwater insects have increased, helped by cleaner rivers. Data are scarce in the tropics, where most insects live, so the global picture is still uncertain.
The main causes
These causes add up. A field sprayed more often, next to a road lit all night, in a hotter summer, offers far less food and shelter than the same place 50 years ago.
What is being done
In 2018 the EU banned outdoor use of three neonicotinoid insecticides harmful to bees. The EU Nature Restoration Law of 2024 includes a goal to reverse pollinator decline by 2030.
Many older drivers recall cleaning dead insects off windscreens after a summer drive; today far fewer get squashed. Scientists call this the "windscreen phenomenon".

deep.w: All insects are disappearing
deep.r: Many species are declining, some are stable and a few are increasing; the overall trend is still a warning

deep.x: Insects are declining from many causes at once, so they need many small fixes at once.

cards.title: Mosquitos
cards.text: Os mosquitos transmitem malária, dengue e outras doenças, o que faz deles o animal mais mortal para os humanos. Só as fêmeas picam; elas precisam de sangue para produzir ovos.

deep.x: There are about 3,500 mosquito species, but only a few hundred bite humans. Only females bite: they need the protein in blood to make eggs. Both sexes otherwise drink plant nectar. A female finds you by your breath, your body heat and the smell of your skin.
Why they're so deadly
A mosquito bite itself is harmless. The danger is what it carries. While feeding, a female can pick up a parasite or virus from one person and pass it to the next.
Malaria still kills about 600,000 people a year, mostly young children in Africa. Dengue infects many millions a year and is spreading as the climate warms.
Portugal's story

Malaria was once common in Portugal's rice fields and river valleys. The WHO declared the country malaria-free in 1973. In 2012 Madeira had a dengue outbreak with over 2,000 cases, spread by an invasive mosquito. The Asian tiger mosquito has been found in mainland Portugal since 2017.

deep.w: Mosquitoes prefer sweet blood
deep.r: What matters is your skin's mix of odours, plus breath and heat

deep.x: The world's deadliest animal is a few milligrams of fly, made dangerous by what it carries.

cards.title: Ajude os insetos em casa
cards.text: Deixe um canto do jardim selvagem, plante flores nativas, dispense os pesticidas, ofereça água e apague as luzes externas desnecessárias.

deep.x: Small spaces add up. Gardens, balconies and roadside verges together cover a large area, and insects need only patches of food and shelter linked together.
Food: plant the right flowers
Native plants suit native insects. In Portugal, rosemary, thyme, French lavender, heather and borage are bee favourites. Aim for something in flower from early spring to late autumn.
Shelter: leave some mess

About seven in ten wild bee species nest in the ground, in bare, sunny soil. Others use hollow stems or holes in dead wood. Leave stems standing over winter, keep a log pile and don't rake every leaf.
Water and light

A shallow dish with pebbles lets bees drink without drowning. At night, white and blue light attracts insects most and confuses moths. Switch off what you don't need, or use warm-coloured bulbs and motion sensors.

x: Mow a 2 m × 3 m patch once a month instead of weekly
Clover and daisies flower
6 m² of food for bees

deep.x: Bought "bee hotels" help only a few species; a patch of bare soil may help more.
Plant native, mow less, skip the sprays and turn off the lights.

quiz.q: Quantas pernas têm os insetos?
quiz.explain: As aranhas têm 8 e não são insetos.

quiz.q: Qual é o animal mais mortal para os humanos?

lessons.title: Mamíferos
lessons.summary: A nossa própria classe de animais.

cards.title: O que faz um mamífero
cards.text: Os mamíferos têm pelos, alimentam os filhotes com leite e têm três ossinhos no ouvido. A maioria dá à luz filhotes vivos.

deep.x: There are about 6,500 living mammal species, from 2-gram shrews to 150-tonne blue whales. The name comes from the Latin mamma, meaning breast; Carl Linnaeus chose it in 1758.
Clues in the ear

The three tiny ear bones are the hammer, anvil and stirrup. Fossils show that two of them began as bones in the jaw joint of our reptile-like ancestors. Over millions of years they shrank and moved into the ear, giving mammals unusually sharp hearing.
Other mammal features

x: Warm-blooded, keeping a steady body temperature (birds do this too)
A diaphragm, a muscle that helps fill the lungs
Different teeth for cutting, tearing and grinding
Long care of the young

deep.x: For more than 100 million years, mammals were mostly small, night-active animals living alongside the dinosaurs. When an asteroid wiped out the large dinosaurs 66 million years ago, mammals spread into the empty roles.

deep.w: Whales and dolphins have no hair, so they aren't mammals
deep.r: They breathe air, make milk, and many have a few bristles, especially when young

deep.x: Milk and hair are the mammal trademarks, but the three ear bones are the deepest clue to our ancestry.

cards.title: Três grupos
cards.text: Os mamíferos placentários desenvolvem os filhotes dentro de uma placenta; os marsupiais, como os cangurus, criam filhotes minúsculos numa bolsa; os monotremados, como o ornitorrinco, põem ovos.

deep.x: All mammals make milk, but they raise their young in three very different ways.
Placentals

Most mammals, including humans, are placentals. The placenta is an organ that links mother and baby, passing food and oxygen in and waste out, so young can grow for a long time inside. Pregnancy lasts from about 16 days in hamsters to about 22 months in elephants.
Marsupials

Marsupials give birth very early. A newborn red kangaroo weighs under 1 gram, about the size of a jelly bean. It crawls through its mother's fur into the pouch, fixes onto a teat and grows there for months. Most marsupials live in Australia and nearby, but about 100 species of opossum live in the Americas.
Monotremes
Only five monotremes survive: the platypus and four species of echidna, all in Australia and New Guinea. They lay leathery eggs, yet still feed their young on milk.

deep.w: Marsupials have no placenta
deep.r: They do have a simple, short-lived one; it just isn't used for long

deep.x: Mammals share milk, but they split three ways on how to get the baby out: early, late or in an egg.

cards.title: O ornitorrinco
cards.text: O ornitorrinco põe ovos, tem um bico parecido com o de um pato que detecta campos elétricos, e os machos têm esporões venenosos. Os primeiros cientistas acharam que era uma farsa.

deep.x: When a dried platypus skin reached Britain in 1799, the naturalist George Shaw wondered if someone had sewn a duck's bill onto a mammal. It was real, and it remains one of the strangest animals alive.
Hunting with a sixth sense

A platypus hunts at the bottom of rivers with its eyes, ears and nostrils shut. Its soft, rubbery bill carries about 40,000 electric sensors. They pick up the tiny electric signals from the muscles of shrimps, worms and insect larvae hidden in the mud.
Milk without nipples
The female lays one to three small eggs in a burrow and keeps them warm for about 10 days. The young lick milk that seeps from patches of skin on her belly, because she has no teats.
Venom
Males have a sharp spur on each hind ankle that delivers venom. It isn't deadly to people, but the pain can last for days or weeks. Males use it mainly against rival males in the breeding season.
Under ultraviolet light, platypus fur glows a blue-green colour, something scientists only reported in 2020.

deep.w: The platypus is half bird, half mammal
deep.r: It's fully a mammal; it just kept old features that most mammals lost

deep.x: The platypus shows what early mammals were like: furry milk-makers that still laid eggs.

cards.title: Morcegos
cards.text: Os morcegos são os únicos mamíferos capazes de voar de verdade e representam cerca de um quinto de todas as espécies de mamíferos. Muitos comem insetos; outros polinizam plantas.

deep.x: There are about 1,400 bat species. Their wings are their hands: thin skin stretched between very long finger bones, which is why the group is called Chiroptera, "hand-wing". Gliding mammals such as flying squirrels can only fall slowly; bats truly fly, flapping and steering.
Seeing with sound
Most insect-eating bats **echolocate**. They make very high-pitched calls, usually beyond human hearing, and listen to the echoes to find moths in the dark.
What bats do for us
A small pipistrelle can eat hundreds of insects in one night. In the United States, bats' pest control has been estimated to be worth billions of dollars a year to farmers.
Bats in Portugal

Portugal has about 27 bat species, all legally protected. In the old university library at Coimbra and the palace library at Mafra, small bats live behind the shelves. At night they hunt the insects that would otherwise eat the books.

deep.w: Bats are blind
deep.r: All bats can see, and fruit bats have large eyes; echolocation adds to sight

deep.x: Bats are flying hands, and they keep the night sky's insects in check.

cards.title: As baleias vieram da terra
cards.text: Os ancestrais das baleias andavam em terra firme há cerca de 50 milhões de anos. Os fósseis mostram as pernas encolhendo aos poucos à medida que se adaptavam à água.

deep.x: Whales, dolphins and porpoises descend from four-legged, hoofed mammals. Their closest living relatives on land are hippos. Fossils found since the 1980s, mostly in Pakistan, India and Egypt, show the move into water step by step.
Clues in living whales

x: Many whales still have small hip bones floating in their bodies
Dolphin embryos briefly grow hind-limb buds, which then disappear
Whales swim by moving the tail up and down, like a running mammal's spine, not side to side like a fish
They breathe air and feed their young on milk

deep.x: Going big
Life in water supports a heavy body, and rich polar seas offer huge amounts of krill. The blue whale, up to about 30 m long, is the largest animal known to have lived.
Whales and dolphins are common off Portugal, especially around the Azores and Madeira, which were once major whaling sites and are now known for whale watching.
The Azores ended commercial whaling in 1987; many former whale lookouts now help guide whale-watching boats.
Whales are mammals that went back to the sea, and their bodies still carry the legs they left behind.

cards.title: Elefantes
cards.text: Os elefantes ficam de luto pelos mortos, se reconhecem no espelho e se comunicam com roncos graves ouvidos a quilômetros de distância.

deep.x: There are three living elephant species: the African savanna elephant, the African forest elephant and the Asian elephant. They are the largest land animals, and among the most socially complex.
Family life

Elephant herds are led by an old female, the **matriarch**. Her memory of water holes and dangers helps the family survive droughts. Pregnancy lasts about 22 months, the longest of any mammal, and calves stay close to their mothers for years.
Talking through the ground
Elephants make deep rumbles, many below the range of human hearing. These can carry several kilometres. Elephants may also pick up vibrations through their feet and trunk.
Minds and mourning

In 2006 an Asian elephant at the Bronx Zoo passed the mirror test: she touched a mark on her head that she could only see in a mirror. Elephants often touch and stand by dead companions, and return to the bones of relatives. Scientists debate whether this is grief like ours, but it clearly shows strong bonds.

deep.w: Elephants are afraid of mice
deep.r: There's no good evidence; they're more likely startled by any small sudden movement

deep.x: Elephants are long-lived, long-memoried families held together by the oldest female.

cards.title: Hibernação
cards.text: Alguns mamíferos sobrevivem ao inverno hibernando: a temperatura do corpo cai, o coração desacelera e eles vivem das reservas de gordura. Os morcegos ibéricos hibernam em cavernas.

deep.x: Staying warm in winter costs a lot of energy, just when food is scarce. Hibernation is a way out: the animal turns its body thermostat down and lives on stored fat.
How deep it goes
A hibernating hedgehog's heart can slow from around 190 to about 20 beats a minute, and its body can cool from 35 °C to a few degrees above the air. Breathing may pause for minutes at a time.
The costly wake-ups

Hibernators don't sleep straight through. Every week or two they warm up for a few hours, perhaps to repair their bodies, then cool down again. These wake-ups use most of the winter's fat. That's why disturbing a hibernating animal can kill it.
Iberian bats in caves

In Portugal, bats such as horseshoe bats and Schreiber's bats gather in caves and old mines that stay cold and steady through winter. A few sites hold thousands of bats, so they are protected and often closed to visitors in winter. Hedgehogs and garden dormice also hibernate in Portugal.
The Arctic ground squirrel can let its body fall below 0 °C during hibernation without freezing.
Hibernation is a planned energy shutdown, and every unplanned wake-up costs fuel the animal can't replace.

cards.title: O lince-ibérico
cards.text: Antes o felino mais ameaçado do mundo, com menos de 100 restantes em 2002, o lince-ibérico se recuperou para mais de 2,000 graças à conservação, inclusive no vale do Guadiana, em Portugal.

deep.x: The Iberian lynx lives only in Spain and Portugal. It weighs about 10 to 13 kg, has tufted ears and a short black-tipped tail, and eats mainly rabbits, which make up around 80 to 90% of its diet.
Brink of extinction

The rabbit crashed twice: myxomatosis arrived in the 1950s and a deadly viral disease in the late 1980s. With habitat loss, hunting and traffic, lynx numbers collapsed. A 2002 count found fewer than 100, in just two small areas of Andalusia.
The comeback

Portugal built a breeding centre near Silves, in the Algarve, which opened in 2009. Since 2015, lynxes have been released in the Guadiana valley around Mértola, where they now breed in the wild. In 2024 the IUCN moved the species from Endangered to Vulnerable.
Still at risk
Road traffic is the main cause of death. Rabbit diseases still threaten the food supply, and the separate populations need to be linked so genes can mix.

deep.w: The lynx is now saved
deep.r: It's much safer, but still Vulnerable and dependent on rabbits and safer roads

deep.x: With breeding, release and rabbits, the Iberian lynx went from fewer than 100 to over 2,000 in about 20 years.

cards.title: Lobos em Portugal
cards.text: O lobo-ibérico sobrevive sobretudo ao norte do Douro, com cerca de 300 em Portugal. É protegido por lei desde 1988.

deep.x: The Iberian wolf is a subspecies of the grey wolf. It's slightly smaller than wolves further north, with dark marks on the front of its forelegs. A century ago wolves lived across most of Portugal; hunting, poisoning and loss of wild prey pushed them back.
Two populations
Most wolves live north of the Douro, in places such as Peneda-Gerês, Montesinho and Alvão. South of the river, a small population is isolated and seriously threatened.
Living with farmers

In northern Portugal, wild prey such as roe deer and wild boar are still recovering, so wolves often take goats, sheep, cattle and the free-roaming garrano ponies. The state pays compensation for confirmed losses. Guard dogs help: traditional breeds such as the Castro Laboreiro dog and the Serra da Estrela mountain dog were bred to protect flocks.

deep.w: Wolves are a danger to people
deep.r: Attacks on people in Portugal are extremely rare; wolves avoid humans

deep.x: Portugal's few hundred wolves survive mainly in the north, where farming and wildlife must share the hills.

cards.title: Primatas
cards.text: Os humanos são primatas, com olhos voltados para a frente, mãos que agarram e cérebros grandes. Nossos parentes vivos mais próximos são os chimpanzés e os bonobos.

deep.x: There are about 500 primate species: lemurs, lorises, monkeys and apes, including us. Most live in tropical forests. Early primates lived in trees, and many of our features are tree-climbing tools.
Our family tree

Humans belong to the great apes, with orangutans, gorillas, chimpanzees and bonobos. Our line split from the chimp line about 6 to 7 million years ago. Chimps and bonobos split from each other only around 1 to 2 million years ago, when the Congo River separated them.
Close cousins
Chimpanzees and humans share about 98 to 99% of their DNA when the genes are lined up. Yet small differences in when and how genes are switched on add up to big differences in body and brain.

x: Chimps hunt in groups, use sticks to fish for termites and can be aggressive
Bonobos settle tension through play and sex and are led by females
Both are Endangered in the wild

deep.x: Europe's only wild primates are the Barbary macaques of Gibraltar, at the southern tip of Iberia.

deep.w: Humans evolved from chimpanzees
deep.r: We share a common ancestor; chimps have been evolving for just as long as we have

deep.x: Humans aren't above the primates; we're one branch of the great-ape family.
