cards.title: O que é um vulcão
cards.text: Um vulcão é uma abertura por onde rocha derretida, gases e cinzas escapam do subsolo. O magma subterrâneo vira lava quando chega à superfície.

deep.x: Deep below the surface, rock is hot but mostly solid. It melts into **magma** when pressure drops, when water is added, or when extra heat arrives from below. Magma is lighter than the rock around it, so it slowly rises, collecting in a magma chamber a few kilometres down.
What comes out

items.b: blobs flung out, cooled in air

deep.x: Lava erupts at about 700–1,200 °C. The gases are a big part of the story: water vapour dissolved in magma behaves like the fizz in a sealed bottle, waiting to escape.
Anatomy of a volcano
There are about 1,350 potentially active volcanoes on land, and somewhere around 50 erupt each year. Many more lie hidden on the seafloor.

deep.w: Lava is the deadliest part of an eruption
deep.r: Most volcanic deaths come from pyroclastic flows (fast avalanches of hot gas and ash) and mudflows

deep.x: A volcano is a leak in the planet's lid, where buoyant, gas-filled magma finally reaches the air.

cards.title: Onde estão os vulcões
cards.text: A maioria dos vulcões fica ao longo dos limites das placas, sobretudo no "Círculo de Fogo" do Pacífico. Outros, como os do Havaí, ficam sobre pontos quentes no meio das placas.

deep.x: Volcanoes aren't scattered randomly. Mapped on a globe, they trace the edges of the tectonic plates, plus a few lonely hotspots.
The Ring of Fire

Around the Pacific, ocean plates dive (subduct) beneath other plates. As the sinking slab heats up, it releases water, which lowers the melting point of the rock above it. The result is a horseshoe of about 40,000 km of volcanoes and earthquakes from New Zealand through Japan and Alaska to the Andes.
Spreading ridges

Where plates pull apart, as along the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, the mantle rises and melts. Most of Earth's lava erupts here, quietly, under the sea. Iceland is a rare spot where the ridge rises above the waves.
Hotspots

Hawaii is thousands of kilometres from a plate edge. A plume of hot mantle rises beneath it, and as the Pacific plate slides over at about 7–10 cm a year, it builds a conveyor belt of islands: young and active in the southeast, old and eroded to the northwest.
Portugal has both kinds of island volcanoes: the Azores sit near the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, while Madeira was built by a hotspot.
Volcanoes mark where plates sink, spread or sit above a plume of hot mantle.

cards.title: Explosivo ou tranquilo
cards.text: A lava basáltica fluida deixa os gases escaparem com suavidade, como no Havaí. O magma viscoso e rico em gases explode, como no Monte Santa Helena ou no Vesúvio.

deep.x: Whether a volcano oozes or explodes depends mostly on how sticky its magma is, and that depends on **silica**. More silica means longer chains of molecules and thicker, stiffer magma.
The fizzy-drink effect

Magma holds dissolved gas under pressure, like an unopened bottle of fizzy drink. In runny basalt, bubbles rise and pop gently, giving lava fountains and rivers. In sticky magma, bubbles can't escape. As the magma rises and pressure falls, they expand violently and shatter the magma into ash.
Measuring the bang
The Volcanic Explosivity Index (VEI) runs from 0 to 8. Each step up means about ten times more material thrown out.
Mount St Helens in the USA blew out its side on 18 May 1980, killing 57 people and removing about 400 m from its summit. Vesuvius in 79 CE was a similar size.
Iceland's Eyjafjallajökull in 2010 was only a modest eruption, but ice meltwater shattered its magma into fine ash that closed much of Europe's airspace for days.
Runny magma lets its gas go; sticky magma traps it until it explodes.

cards.title: Pompeia
cards.text: Em 79 d.C., o Vesúvio soterrou Pompeia e Herculano sob as cinzas, preservando uma cidade romana com detalhes impressionantes.

deep.x: In 79 CE, Vesuvius had been quiet for centuries. Many Romans didn't even know it was a volcano. Then it erupted for about a day, and two towns on the Bay of Naples vanished.
A letter from the scene

Pliny the Younger watched from across the bay and later described it in two letters to the historian Tacitus. His uncle, Pliny the Elder, commander of the Roman fleet, died trying to rescue people. Volcanologists still call this kind of tall, explosive column a **Plinian eruption**.
Two towns, two fates

At Pompeii, ash hardened around victims' bodies. In 1863 the archaeologist Giuseppe Fiorelli poured plaster into the hollows they left, creating the famous casts. Herculaneum preserved wooden furniture, food and a library of carbonised papyrus scrolls. Since 2023, researchers have used X-ray scans and AI to begin reading text from scrolls that cannot be unrolled.
Most people in Pompeii probably escaped. Remains of over a thousand victims have been found, out of a population thought to be at least 10,000.
An inscription found in 2018 suggests the eruption happened in October, not on 24 August as long believed.
Pompeii is a city frozen in a single day, and Vesuvius, which still has hundreds of thousands of people living on its slopes, is still active.

cards.title: Os Açores

events.l: terremoto de Vila Franca do Campo

cards.text: Os Açores ficam onde três placas se encontram. O vulcão dos Capelinhos, no Faial, entrou em erupção em 1957–58, acrescentando terra nova à ilha.

deep.x: The Azores sit on a **triple junction**, where the North American, Eurasian and Nubian (African) plates meet. The Mid-Atlantic Ridge runs just west of the central islands, and a slow, messy rift cuts through the archipelago. Add a possible mantle plume underneath, and you get nine volcanic islands and frequent earthquakes.
Capelinhos, 1957–58

On 27 September 1957, the sea began to boil off the western tip of Faial. For about 13 months, an underwater eruption grew into a new volcano, joined Faial and added roughly 2.4 km² of land. Ash buried farms and houses, and the lighthouse was half swallowed.

The disaster triggered a wave of emigration. A US law of 1958, co-sponsored by Senator John F. Kennedy, allowed thousands of Azoreans to settle in America. Today the buried lighthouse houses an underground interpretation centre.
Living with volcanoes

x: Furnas, on São Miguel, cooks its famous stew (cozido) in pots buried in hot volcanic ground
Geothermal power plants on São Miguel supply roughly 40% of the island's electricity
Pico, Portugal's highest mountain, last erupted in the 1700s
CIVISA monitors the islands' earthquakes and volcanoes around the clock

deep.x: Much of the land Capelinhos added has since been eroded by Atlantic waves, a reminder of how fast new volcanic land can disappear.
The Azores are Portugal's living geology lab, where three plates meet and new land can still rise from the sea.

cards.title: Como acontecem os terremotos
cards.text: As rochas ao longo de uma falha ficam travadas enquanto as placas continuam se movendo. A tensão se acumula até que elas deslizam de repente, liberando energia na forma de ondas sísmicas.

deep.x: Tectonic plates move about 2–10 cm a year, about as fast as your fingernails grow. But along a fault, the rocks on either side are jammed together by friction. The plates keep moving, so the rock bends and stores energy like a drawn bow.

When the stress overcomes friction, the fault slips in seconds, sometimes by several metres. The stored energy radiates out as **seismic waves**. This idea, called elastic rebound, came from studying the 1906 San Francisco earthquake.
The waves

The point underground where the slip begins is the **focus** (or hypocentre); the point on the surface directly above it is the **epicentre**. The gap between P and S wave arrivals tells seismologists how far away a quake was.
Portugal's quake history

Portugal lies near the boundary between the Eurasian and Nubian plates, which runs from the Azores to the Strait of Gibraltar. On 1 November 1755 an offshore earthquake, estimated at magnitude 8.5–9, followed by a tsunami and fires, destroyed much of Lisbon and killed tens of thousands of people. Smaller quakes are felt in the Algarve and Lisbon regions every few years.
The 1755 Lisbon earthquake helped launch modern seismology: the Marquis of Pombal sent a questionnaire to every parish asking what people had seen.
An earthquake is the sudden release of strain that slowly built up while a stuck fault waited to slip.

cards.title: Medir terremotos
cards.text: A escala de magnitude de momento é logarítmica: cada grau a mais libera cerca de 32 vezes mais energia. Um terremoto de magnitude 7 libera cerca de 1,000 vezes mais que um de 5.

deep.x: The first famous scale came from Charles Richter in 1935. Today seismologists use the **moment magnitude** scale, which measures the real size of the event: how big an area of fault slipped, how far, and how stiff the rock was.
Why the numbers are deceptive
The scale is logarithmic. Each step up means the ground shakes about ten times harder on a seismograph and releases about 32 times more energy.

x: Magnitude 5 to 6
×32 energy
Magnitude 5 to 7

deep.x: Magnitude versus intensity

A magnitude 6 under a city can do more harm than a magnitude 8 far out at sea. Intensity scales, like the European Macroseismic Scale used in Portugal, rate shaking from I (not felt) to XII (complete destruction).

deep.w: A magnitude 8 is twice as strong as a magnitude 4
deep.r: It releases about a million times more energy

deep.x: On the magnitude scale, every two steps up means roughly a thousand times more energy.

cards.title: Tsunamis

steps: O fundo do mar se sacode

cards.text: Terremotos submarinos podem levantar o fundo do mar, empurrando para cima toda a coluna de água. As ondas de tsunami viajam à velocidade de um avião a jato em águas profundas e crescem perto da costa.

deep.x: A tsunami is not a giant surfing wave. When an undersea earthquake suddenly lifts or drops the seafloor, it moves the entire column of water above it, from the bottom to the surface. That creates waves with wavelengths of hundreds of kilometres.
Jet speed in deep water
A tsunami's speed depends only on the depth of the water.

x: Ocean 4,000 m deep
about 700 km/h, as fast as a jet

deep.x: In deep water the wave may be less than a metre tall, so ships barely notice. As it reaches shallow water it slows, the back catches up with the front, and the water heaps up, sometimes 10–30 m high.
Not just one wave
Tsunamis come as a series of waves, often 10 to 60 minutes apart, and the first is often not the biggest. They can also be caused by landslides, volcanic eruptions or meteorite impacts.
The 1755 tsunami reached Lisbon's riverside about 40 minutes after the earthquake, catching people who had fled to the open quays for safety.
A tsunami moves the whole ocean, not just its surface, which is why it travels so fast and hits so hard.

cards.title: Sinais de alerta
cards.text: Se o mar recuar de repente para longe da praia, pode vir um tsunami: vá imediatamente para um lugar alto. Portugal tem placas de aviso de tsunami no litoral.

deep.x: Official warning systems help, but for a tsunami generated close to shore, nature's own warnings may be all you get. Near Portugal, a big offshore quake could send waves to the Algarve in 15–30 minutes.
Why the sea retreats

If the trough of the wave arrives first, the water is drawn out before the crest hits. Reefs, rocks and fish are left exposed, and curious people walk out to look. This is the worst possible reaction: the wave may arrive within minutes.

items.w: Go and look at the sea

items.r: Shaking or drawback is the alert

deep.x: What to do

x: Move inland or uphill immediately, on foot if roads are jammed
Aim for ground at least 30 m above sea level, or 2–3 km inland
If you can't get away, go to an upper floor of a solid concrete building
Stay away until authorities say it's safe; later waves can be bigger

deep.x: Since the 2010s, Portuguese coastal towns such as Cascais, Lisbon and several in the Algarve have put up blue tsunami signs marking risk zones and evacuation routes. IPMA monitors earthquakes and issues tsunami alerts.
In 2004, a 10-year-old British girl on a Thai beach recognised the retreating sea from a school geography lesson and warned her family; around a hundred people were evacuated safely.
If the ground shakes hard or the sea draws back, don't wait: get to high ground.

cards.title: Vulcões e clima
cards.text: Erupções enormes lançam enxofre bem alto na atmosfera, resfriando o planeta. Depois do Tambora, em 1815, 1816 ficou conhecido como o "ano sem verão".

deep.x: The ash from a big eruption falls out within weeks. The climate effect comes from **sulphur dioxide**. Blasted into the stratosphere, above the weather, it forms tiny droplets of sulphuric acid that reflect sunlight back to space for one to three years.
The year without a summer

Tambora, in Indonesia, erupted in April 1815, the largest eruption in recorded history. It killed tens of thousands locally. The next year, northern hemisphere summers were cold and wet: frosts in June in New England, crop failures across Europe, food riots and famine.
That gloomy summer of 1816, Mary Shelley, stuck indoors by storms at Lake Geneva, began writing *Frankenstein*.
Do volcanoes cause global warming?
Volcanoes release CO2, but far less than people do. All the world's volcanoes together emit well under 1 gigatonne a year; human activity emits around 37 gigatonnes of CO2 from fossil fuels alone.

deep.w: Volcanoes emit more CO2 than humans
deep.r: Humans emit roughly 100 times more each year

deep.x: Big eruptions cool the planet for a few years by veiling the Sun with sulphur haze; they don't drive long-term warming.

quiz.q: Onde ocorre a maioria dos vulcões?
options: Ao longo dos limites das placas

quiz.q: Um recuo repentino do mar na praia pode indicar…

cards.title: Intemperismo e erosão
cards.text: A chuva, o gelo, o vento e as raízes quebram as rochas (intemperismo), e a água, o gelo e o vento levam os pedaços embora (erosão). Com tempo, eles aplainam montanhas.

deep.x: Rock seems permanent, but given time it always loses. **Weathering** breaks rock down where it sits; **erosion** carries the pieces away. Together they wear down every mountain and feed every beach.
How rock breaks

x: Freeze–thaw: water seeps into cracks and expands by about 9% when it freezes, wedging rock apart
Chemical: slightly acidic rain dissolves limestone and turns minerals in granite into clay
Biological: tree roots prise open cracks; lichens release acids

deep.x: Granite landscapes in Portugal, like Monsanto or the Serra da Estrela, show this well: weathering along cracks leaves huge rounded boulders stacked on top of each other.
How pieces move
Rivers do most of the transport, but glaciers, wind, waves and gravity (landslides) all help.

x: Mountain wears down 0.1 mm a year
over 10 million years
0.1 mm × 10,000,000 = 1,000 m, a whole mountain gone

deep.x: The Colorado River has carved the Grand Canyon, about 1.8 km deep, in roughly the last 5–6 million years.
Tiny losses every year, multiplied by millions of years, are enough to erase mountains.

cards.title: As montanhas se erguem
cards.text: As montanhas se formam onde as placas colidem e a crosta se dobra para cima. O Himalaia ainda sobe alguns milímetros por ano, à medida que a Índia empurra a Ásia.

deep.x: Most great mountain ranges are made by collisions. When two continents meet, neither sinks easily, so the crust crumples, folds and thickens, pushing rock up into peaks and down into deep roots.
The Himalayas

India broke away from the southern supercontinent and raced north. Around 50 million years ago it hit Asia. It is still pushing north by about 4–5 cm a year, and the Himalayas are still rising by a few millimetres a year, though erosion and earthquakes take some back.
Kinds of mountains

Mountains also float, in a way. Thick crust sits deeper in the denser mantle beneath, like an iceberg. As the tops erode, the roots slowly bob up, so mountains keep rising for a while even after collision stops.
The Pyrenees formed when the Iberian plate pushed into Europe. The same squeeze helped lift Portugal's Serra da Estrela, part of a chain of ranges running across central Iberia.
The rock at the summit of Everest is marine limestone, full of fossils of sea creatures that lived on an ocean floor.
Mountains are the crumple zone of colliding plates, and the collision that built the Himalayas is still going on.

cards.title: A viagem de um rio
cards.text: Os rios mudam ao longo do caminho: íngremes, rápidos e estreitos perto da nascente; largos e lentos perto da foz, onde depositam sedimentos.

deep.x: Geographers divide a river into three stretches. Each has its own job: cutting down, cutting sideways, or dropping its load.
Upper course

Near the source, the river is small but steep. It carries big boulders that grind its bed, cutting a narrow V-shaped valley. Waterfalls and rapids form where hard rock resists. Many northern Portuguese rivers, like the Paiva, have these wild, rocky stretches.
Middle and lower course

Further down, more tributaries join, so the river carries more water. It starts to swing side to side, widening its valley. Near the sea, the land is flat; the river spreads over a floodplain, and when it slows at the mouth it drops its sediment in a delta or an estuary like the Tejo's.
Load and discharge
Rivers move rock in three ways: rolling boulders along the bed, carrying sand and silt suspended in the water, and dissolving minerals invisibly.

deep.w: Rivers flow fastest in their steep upper course
deep.r: Average speed often increases downstream: there's more water and less friction, even if it looks calmer

deep.x: A river is a conveyor belt that cuts in the hills and builds in the lowlands.

cards.title: Meandros
cards.text: Os rios erodem o lado de fora das curvas e depositam do lado de dentro, então as curvas crescem. Por fim, um laço fica isolado, formando um lago em ferradura.

deep.x: Even a straight river doesn't stay straight. Any small bend makes water swing to the outside, and that starts a feedback loop.
How a bend grows

As water rounds a curve, it piles up against the outer bank and spirals down and across to the inner bank, carrying sediment with it. The outer bank is eaten away; the inner bank builds up. The bend becomes a loop, and the whole meander slowly migrates downstream.
The oxbow lake

Eventually two bends almost touch. In a flood, the river takes the short cut across the narrow neck. Sediment seals off the old loop, leaving a curved lake: an **oxbow lake**. Over time, it fills with plants and silt and becomes a marsh.

x: River winds 15 km to cover 10 km
sinuosity = 15 ÷ 10 = 1.5
above about 1.5, a river counts as meandering

deep.x: The word "meander" comes from the Büyük Menderes River in Turkey, known to the ancient Greeks as the Maeander for its winding course.
Erosion on the outside and deposition on the inside make river bends grow until they're cut off as oxbow lakes.

cards.title: Geleiras
cards.text: As geleiras escavam vales em forma de U e deixam montes de detritos chamados morenas. A Serra da Estrela foi moldada por geleiras na última era glacial.

deep.x: A glacier is a river of ice. Snow piles up faster than it melts, gets compressed into dense ice, and then flows downhill under its own weight, typically tens of metres to a few hundred metres a year.
How ice carves

x: Plucking: ice freezes onto rock and tears blocks away as it moves
Abrasion: rocks embedded in the ice scrape the valley like sandpaper
Transport: ice carries everything from sand to house-sized boulders

deep.x: What glaciers leave behind
Ice in Portugal

About 20,000 years ago, at the peak of the last ice age, an ice cap covered the high plateau of the Serra da Estrela, and glaciers flowed down its valleys. The Zêzere valley above Manteigas is a textbook U-shaped glacial valley, and moraines and glacier-polished rocks can be seen along its trails. Lakes such as Lagoa Comprida sit in hollows carved by ice.
At the height of the last ice age, so much water was locked in ice that sea level was about 120 m lower, and Portugal's coastline lay many kilometres further west.
Glaciers turn V-shaped river valleys into broad U-shapes, and the Serra da Estrela still wears their marks.

cards.title: Cavernas
cards.text: A água da chuva, levemente ácida, dissolve aos poucos o calcário, formando cavernas. A água que pinga deixa estalactites penduradas e estalagmites crescendo do chão.

deep.x: Rain picks up carbon dioxide from the air and, even more, from soil. That makes a weak acid, carbonic acid. Limestone is made of calcium carbonate, which this acid slowly dissolves.
water + carbon dioxide → carbonic acid, which dissolves limestone
Decorating the cave

When water seeps into an air-filled cave, it releases some of its CO2, just like a fizzy drink going flat. It can no longer hold all its dissolved calcium carbonate, so it leaves a thin film of crystal behind. Drip by drip, formations grow.

x: Typical growth 0.1 mm a year

deep.x: Caves in Portugal

The limestone Serras de Aire e Candeeiros, in central Portugal, are riddled with caves. The Grutas de Mira de Aire, discovered in 1947, are the country's largest known cave system, with over 11 km of passages. Landscapes like this, with sinkholes, underground rivers and few surface streams, are called **karst**.
A memory trick: stalac**t**ites hold **t**ight to the ceiling; stalag**m**ites **m**ight reach them one day.
Caves are carved by a weak acid in rainwater and decorated by the same water giving back its stone.

cards.title: Litorais
cards.text: As ondas erodem os promontórios e criam grutas, arcos e leixões. As falésias douradas e os rochedos isolados no mar do Algarve são exemplos clássicos.

deep.x: Waves are the sculptors of the coast. They hurl water and pebbles at cliffs and squeeze air into cracks, which then explodes outward as the wave retreats. Softer rock and lines of weakness give way first.
The Algarve's showcase

The western Algarve's golden cliffs are made of relatively soft limestone and sandstone, laid down in a shallow sea millions of years ago. Around Lagos, Ponta da Piedade is a maze of arches, stacks and grottoes. Near Lagoa, the Benagil sea cave has a hole in its roof where part of the ceiling collapsed.
Erosion and deposition

Where waves lose energy, they drop sand. The Ria Formosa lagoon near Faro is protected by a chain of sandy barrier islands, and the Tróia peninsula is a long sand spit built across the mouth of the Sado.
Cliffs are unstable

Cliffs retreat in sudden collapses, not gradually. In 2009, part of a cliff at Praia Maria Luísa near Albufeira fell onto the beach and killed five people. That's why Portuguese beaches have signs telling you to keep away from the base and edge of cliffs.
Sea arches are temporary: most collapse within a few centuries or less, and the stacks standing off the Algarve today were once arches.
Waves turn headlands into caves, arches, stacks and stumps, and dump the eroded sand on calmer shores.

cards.title: Desertos
cards.text: Os desertos recebem menos de cerca de 250 mm de chuva por ano. Só cerca de um quinto dos desertos do mundo é de areia; a maioria é de rocha e cascalho. A Antártida é o maior deserto.

deep.x: A desert is defined by dryness, not heat or sand. The usual rule of thumb is less than about 250 mm of precipitation a year, or more water evaporating than falling. By that measure, about a third of Earth's land is arid or semi-arid.
Hot and cold

Most hot deserts sit around 20–30° from the equator, under belts of sinking, dry air. Others are in the "rain shadow" of mountains or next to cold ocean currents, like the Atacama in Chile, where some weather stations have recorded almost no rain for years.
Mostly not sand

Only about a fifth of the world's deserts are sand seas (ergs). The rest is bare rock, gravel plains, salt flats and mountains. Desert temperatures can swing by 30 °C between day and night, because dry air and clear skies let heat escape fast.
Parts of southern Portugal's interior are classified as at risk of desertification, as drought, heat and soil erosion combine.
A desert is any place starved of precipitation, which is why ice-covered Antarctica is the biggest of all.

cards.title: Os rios de Portugal
cards.text: O Tejo é o rio mais longo da Península Ibérica, com cerca de 1,000 km. O vale íngreme do Douro abriga a região vinícola demarcada mais antiga do mundo, de 1756.

deep.x: Portugal's great rivers mostly start in Spain and flow west to the Atlantic. That means water management is shared: the 1998 Albufeira Convention sets how much water Spain must let through on shared rivers.
The Tejo

The Tagus rises in the mountains east of Madrid and runs about 1,000 km to Lisbon. Only about the last quarter is in Portugal. Its estuary is one of the largest in Europe and makes Lisbon one of the world's great natural harbours. The Mondego is the longest river entirely within Portugal.
The Douro

The Douro cuts a deep, steep valley through hard schist and granite. Over centuries, people built terraces on the slopes to grow vines. In 1756, the Marquis of Pombal set boundaries for where port wine grapes could be grown, making the Douro the world's oldest legally demarcated wine region.
Dams and reservoirs
Most big Portuguese rivers are now chains of dams, providing hydropower and irrigation. The Alqueva reservoir on the Guadiana, about 250 km², is one of the largest artificial lakes in Western Europe.
Before dams were built, the Douro was so wild that port wine was taken downstream to Porto on flat-bottomed rabelo boats through dangerous rapids.
Portugal's rivers are borrowed from Spain, shaped its wine and its capital, and are now tamed by dams.

cards.title: Os pontos mais altos
cards.text: O ponto mais alto de Portugal é a Montanha do Pico, nos Açores, com 2,351 m, um vulcão. No continente, a Torre, na Serra da Estrela, chega a 1,993 m.

deep.x: Portugal's highest mountain isn't on the mainland at all. **Mount Pico**, on the Azores island of the same name, is a volcano rising to 2,351 m. It also rises from a seafloor more than 1,000 m below sea level, so its full height is far greater than what you see.
Climbing Pico

Pico is a young volcano that last erupted in the early 1700s. Hikers register before climbing and usually take about 3–4 hours to reach the summit, where a small cone called Piquinho still releases warm volcanic gas. On clear days you can see São Jorge and Faial.
Torre and the Serra da Estrela

On the mainland, the top of the Serra da Estrela, called Torre, reaches 1,993 m. The name "Torre" (tower) comes from a stone monument built on the summit in the early 19th century, said to have been raised so the top would reach a round 2,000 m.
The Serra da Estrela is the only place in mainland Portugal with a ski station, and it has some of the country's coldest winter temperatures.
Pico's summit is often the only part of the Azores poking above the clouds, and in winter it is frequently capped with snow.
Portugal's rooftop is an Atlantic volcano; the mainland's high point is a granite plateau once capped by ice.

quiz.q: O que forma um lago em ferradura?
quiz.explain: As curvas crescem até que um laço fica isolado.

quiz.q: Qual é o maior deserto do mundo?
quiz.explain: Os desertos são definidos pela pouca precipitação.

lessons.title: Fungos: o reino escondido
lessons.summary: Micélio, cogumelos, parceiros das raízes, leveduras, remédios, líquens e os gigantes escondidos debaixo da terra.

cards.title: Nem planta nem animal

deep.x: Early naturalists, from Aristotle to Linnaeus in the 18th century, filed fungi under plants. Only in 1969 did the American ecologist Robert Whittaker give them a kingdom of their own, and DNA studies later confirmed that fungi are closer to animals.
Eating from the outside

A fungus grows into its food, then pours out digestive enzymes. These break big molecules such as cellulose and proteins into small ones that the fungus absorbs through its cell walls. In effect it lives inside its own stomach.
Three ways of life

x: Decomposers feed on dead wood, leaves and dung
Parasites attack living hosts: chestnut blight, athlete's foot, the "zombie-ant" fungus
Partners trade with plants or algae, as in mycorrhiza and lichens

deep.x: Fungi cause most plant diseases and some serious human infections, but most species are harmless to us, and many are essential to ecosystems.
Some fungi are hunters: the oyster mushroom can paralyse and digest tiny roundworms in the wood it grows on.
Fungi are nature's great absorbers: they digest the world from the outside in.

cards.text:
Os fungos formam o seu próprio reino da vida, separado das plantas e dos animais. Eles não conseguem produzir alimento a partir da luz do sol; em vez disso, liberam enzimas e absorvem o que digerem fora do próprio corpo.

O grupo inclui cogumelos, bolores e leveduras. Os cientistas já deram nome a cerca de 150,000 espécies, mas pode haver milhões a mais.

cards.title: Micélio, o corpo escondido

deep.x: Each hypha is a tube a few thousandths of a millimetre wide, far thinner than a human hair. Because it grows only at the tip, it can push its way into wood and between soil grains. A single gram of forest soil can hold tens to hundreds of metres of hyphae.
A network that adapts

When one part of a mycelium finds food, it thickens the threads leading there and lets unproductive ones die back. In lab experiments, wood-rotting fungi given scattered food sources built networks that balanced efficiency and resilience, rather like well-designed transport systems.
Long-lived and hard to see

A mycelium can live for years or centuries, producing mushrooms only when conditions suit. Fairy rings, circles of mushrooms in grass, form as a mycelium grows outward from a centre, using up nutrients behind it. Some rings in Europe are thought to be hundreds of years old.
Mycelium as a material
Grown on farm waste, mycelium binds loose material into light, solid shapes, and some fungi can be grown as food.

deep.w: A mushroom is the whole fungus
deep.r: It is a short-lived fruiting body; the mycelium is the real, long-lived organism

deep.x: The real fungus is the hidden web, not the mushroom you see.

cards.text:
O corpo principal de um fungo é o micélio, uma rede de filamentos microscópicos chamados hifas. Ele se espalha pelo solo, pela madeira, pelas folhas caídas ou pelos alimentos, quase sempre longe da vista.

As hifas crescem pelas pontas e podem se fundir umas com as outras, formando redes que exploram o solo em busca de alimento.

cards.title: Os cogumelos são frutos

items: O pé os ergue no ar

deep.x: Mushrooms often spring up after autumn rain because they grow mostly by swelling, not by making new cells. The mycelium prepares a tiny knot of tissue underground, then pumps water into it. That is why mushrooms can even push up through tarmac.
Launching spores

Many mushrooms launch their spores with a drop of water that forms beside each spore. When the drop suddenly merges with a film on the spore, the shift in weight flicks it away with an acceleration thousands of times that of gravity. It travels only a fraction of a millimetre, just enough to fall clear of the gill and drift away.
Many shapes

Truffles grow underground and cannot use the wind. Instead they give off strong smells that attract animals, which dig them up, eat them and spread the spores in their droppings. That is why pigs and trained dogs can find them.
Spore prints
Placing a cap gills-down on paper overnight leaves a spore print. Its colour, from white or pink to brown or black, is one of many features experts use in identification, never on its own.
Some mushrooms make their own wind: water evaporating from the cap cools the air beneath it, creating gentle currents that lift spores even on still days.
A mushroom is a temporary launch pad, built fast to send spores out into the world.

cards.text:
Um cogumelo é um corpo de frutificação: a parte que o fungo constrói para espalhar os seus esporos. Ele pode aparecer de um dia para o outro porque enche de água células que já estavam formadas.

Um único cogumelo pode liberar bilhões de esporos microscópicos, levados pelo ar, pela água e pelos animais.

cards.title: Decompor a madeira

deep.x: Wood is mostly cellulose fibres, glued and armoured with lignin. Many organisms can digest cellulose, but lignin is a jumble of chemical rings that few enzymes can attack. White-rot fungi produce powerful oxidising enzymes that tear it apart, which is why rotten logs eventually crumble.
A coal mystery

Much of the world's coal formed about 360 to 300 million years ago, in the Carboniferous period. One hypothesis says this happened partly because fungi able to digest lignin had not yet evolved, so dead trees piled up. Other scientists argue that vast swamps, climate and moving continents explain it better. The debate continues.

items.w: No fungi ate wood, so coal formed
items.r: Fungi may be part of it; swamps mattered

deep.x: Decay at work

x: Shelf fungi on dead trunks are the fruiting bodies of wood-rotters
Rotting wood left in forests shelters beetles, birds and bats
Compost heaps rely on fungi to break down woody stems and paper

deep.x: When decay hits our homes

The same skills cause trouble indoors. Dry rot, Serpula lacrymans, can spread through damp timber in old buildings and destroy floors and roofs. Keeping wood dry is the best defence, because fungi need moisture to grow.
Some white-rot fungi can also break down pollutants such as certain dyes and pesticides, and are being tested to clean up contaminated soil.
Fungi are the recyclers that can fully unlock wood, returning a tree's carbon and nutrients to the cycle.

cards.text:
A madeira é difícil de digerir por causa da lignina, um material resistente que endurece as paredes das células vegetais. Os fungos são os principais organismos capazes de decompô-la por completo.

Sem eles, as árvores mortas se acumulariam por séculos, e o carbono e os nutrientes presos nelas demorariam a voltar ao solo e ao ar.

cards.title: Parceiros das raízes

deep.x: Fossils from Scotland's Rhynie chert, about 400 million years old, show fungi inside the cells of some of the earliest land plants. Many scientists think this partnership helped plants leave the water: the first plants had no true roots, and fungi did much of the job.
How the trade works

Fungal threads are far thinner than roots and reach into the tiniest pores of soil. They release acids and enzymes that free phosphorus locked in minerals. In exchange, a plant may pass a sizeable share of its sugars, by some estimates up to about a fifth, to its fungal partners.
Orchids, truffles and pines

x: Orchid seeds are as fine as dust and cannot sprout without a fungus feeding them
Truffles are the fruiting bodies of fungi partnered with oak and hazel roots
Pines planted in new continents often grew poorly until the right fungi arrived

deep.x: What about the "wood wide web"?

Fungal networks can link several trees at once. But claims that trees use them to feed their young or send warnings have been questioned: a 2023 review found the evidence weaker than popular books suggest. The partnership is solid; a forest-wide "internet" remains a hypothesis.
Most plants on Earth grow with fungal partners underground, a trade at least 400 million years old.

cards.text:
A maioria das plantas terrestres, cerca de 80–90% das espécies, vive em parceria com fungos dentro e em volta das raízes, a chamada micorriza. Os filamentos dos fungos estendem o alcance das raízes bem fundo no solo.

A planta paga com açúcares da fotossíntese. Os fungos trazem água e nutrientes como o fósforo, e podem ajudar as plantas a enfrentar a seca e as doenças.

cards.title: Líquens: uma parceria

deep.x: In 1867 the Swiss botanist Simon Schwendener proposed that lichens were partnerships, an idea many experts at first rejected. In 2016 researchers found that many lichens also contain a third partner, a yeast, in their outer layer. A lichen is better thought of as a tiny ecosystem.
Pioneers

About 20,000 lichen species are known. They survive drying out completely and spring back to life with rain. On bare rock they slowly release acids that help break it down, starting the first soil. Some grow a millimetre or less a year, and some crusts are thousands of years old.
Pollution detectors

Many lichens absorb water and nutrients straight from the air, so they also take in pollutants. Shaggy, bushy lichens disappear first where sulphur dioxide is high; tough, crusty ones hang on. In many European cities lichens have returned as coal smoke declined.
Useful lichens

x: "Reindeer moss" is a lichen and a key winter food for reindeer
Litmus, the classic acid–alkali indicator, comes from lichens
Lichens were long used to dye wool, including traditional Scottish tweed

deep.x: The grey-green beard-like tufts hanging from trees in clean, damp hills, such as those of northern Portugal, are lichens of the genus Usnea.
A lichen is a partnership so close that it behaves like one organism and survives where neither partner could alone.

cards.text:
Um líquen parece um único organismo, mas é uma parceria: um fungo que vive com algas ou cianobactérias. O fungo dá abrigo; o parceiro produz alimento a partir da luz do sol.

Juntos, eles crescem em rocha nua, cascas de árvore, telhados e tundra, dos desertos à Antártida. Muitos são sensíveis à poluição do ar.

cards.title: A levedura, uma pequena operária

deep.x: A yeast cell is about five thousandths of a millimetre across, and a small block of fresh baker's yeast contains billions of them. They multiply by budding: a small bulge grows on the cell, receives a copy of its DNA and pinches off.
Lager's surprise ancestor

Lager yeast is a hybrid of brewer's yeast and a cold-loving wild species. That second parent was a mystery until 2011, when scientists found it on southern beech trees in Patagonia. How it reached Europe's breweries is still debated.
A model for our own cells

Yeast cells have a nucleus and many of the same genes as human cells, but they grow fast and are easy to study. In 1996 yeast became the first organism with a nucleus to have its whole genome read. Yeast research helped win Nobel Prizes for discoveries about cell division in 2001 and about how cells recycle their parts in 2016.
Yeast factories

x: Engineered yeast makes a large share of the world's insulin
A hepatitis B vaccine has been produced in yeast since the 1980s
Yeast also makes flavours, enzymes and some biofuels

deep.x: Yeast is so like us that some human genes can replace their yeast versions and keep the cells alive.
Yeast is both one of humanity's oldest helpers and one of its most modern tools.

cards.text:
As leveduras são fungos unicelulares. Uma espécie, a Saccharomyces cerevisiae, trabalha para os humanos há milhares de anos, fazendo o pão crescer e fermentando cerveja e vinho.

Hoje ela também é um dos organismos de laboratório mais importantes da biologia, e é modificada para produzir remédios como a insulina e vacinas.

cards.title: Remédios vindos de bolores

deep.x: In the soil, fungi compete with bacteria for food, and many produce substances that kill or slow their rivals. Alexander Fleming noticed this in 1928, when a mould contaminating a dish of bacteria cleared a ring around itself. Turning it into a medicine took Howard Florey, Ernst Chain and their Oxford team until the early 1940s.
Finding better moulds

Early penicillin was made in tiny amounts. In 1943, in Peoria in the USA, a mould on a cantaloupe melon from a local market turned out to produce far more. Its descendants, improved further in the lab, made penicillin cheap enough for millions, and fungi are still grown in huge steel tanks to make it.
Beyond penicillin

Cephalosporins, another major family of antibiotics, came from a mould found near a sewage outlet in Sardinia in 1948. Ciclosporin, from a fungus in a Norwegian soil sample, calms the immune system and made organ transplants far more successful from the 1980s. The first statins were discovered in fungi by the Japanese scientist Akira Endo in the 1970s.
A double edge
Some fungal chemicals are poisons. The ergot fungus on rye caused outbreaks of poisoning in medieval Europe, yet its compounds later gave medicines for migraine and for bleeding after childbirth.
Some of medicine's most important drugs are weapons that fungi evolved against their rivals.

cards.text:
Os fungos combatem as bactérias e uns aos outros com substâncias químicas, e algumas viraram remédios que salvam vidas. A penicilina, de um bolor Penicillium, deu início à era dos antibióticos.

Outras moléculas de fungos hoje evitam a rejeição de órgãos transplantados e baixam o colesterol. A busca por novos medicamentos nos fungos continua.

cards.title: O fungo gigantesco

deep.x: Foresters noticed patches of dying conifers in the Malheur National Forest. Around 2000, scientists sampled the fungus at many points and compared their DNA. Samples across the whole area were genetically identical, meaning they belonged to one individual that had grown outwards for millennia.
How it spreads

Honey fungus sends out black, root-like cords called rhizomorphs, nicknamed "bootlaces", which grow through the soil from tree to tree. It invades roots, kills many trees and then feeds on the dead wood. Under the bark of infected trees lie white sheets of mycelium that smell of mushrooms.
Measuring a giant
Its age is estimated from its growth rate, at somewhere between about 2,000 and 8,000 years. Its weight is unknown, and which organism counts as "largest" depends on whether you measure area or mass.
Closer to home

Honey fungi are common across Europe, including Portugal, where they attack fruit trees, vines, chestnuts and garden shrubs. Gardeners recognise them by the bootlaces and the clusters of mushrooms at the base of dying trees.
Honey fungus mycelium glows faintly in the dark, the "foxfire" sometimes seen on rotting wood at night.
One fungus can quietly occupy an entire forest, visible only as a few mushrooms each autumn.

cards.text:
Nas Blue Mountains do Oregon, nos EUA, um único fungo-do-mel, Armillaria ostoyae, se espalha debaixo da floresta por quase 10 quilômetros quadrados. Ele pode ter vários milhares de anos.

Em área, é um dos maiores organismos vivos conhecidos. Acima do solo, só se veem tufos de cogumelos cor de mel no outono.

cards.title: Comestível ou mortal?

items.w: Os animais comem, então é seguro
items.r: Muitos animais toleram os nossos venenos
As toxinas mortais resistem ao cozimento

deep.x: The death cap looks harmless: a greenish cap, white gills and a ring on the stem, with a cup-like sac at its base that is often hidden in the soil. Its toxins, called amatoxins, are not destroyed by cooking, freezing or drying, and a single mushroom can be enough to kill an adult.
Why it is so dangerous

Symptoms start late, often after 6 to 12 hours or more, when the toxins are already in the body. A false recovery can follow before the liver fails. Fast hospital treatment saves many lives, so act at once if poisoning is possible.
Myths that kill

x: A silver spoon does not turn black near poisonous mushrooms
Peeling the cap does not remove the toxins
A pleasant smell or taste proves nothing
Mushrooms growing on wood or nibbled by slugs can still be toxic

deep.x: In Portugal

Autumn brings mushroom fairs and guided walks, especially in Trás-os-Montes and the Beiras, where ceps, chanterelles and Caesar's mushrooms are prized. If you suspect poisoning, call the Antipoison Information Centre (CIAV) on 800 250 250 or 112, and keep any leftover mushrooms for identification.

deep.w: Poisonous mushrooms are brightly coloured
deep.r: The deadliest, like the death cap and the destroying angel, are pale and plain-looking

deep.x: With wild mushrooms, the only safe rule is expert identification, every single time.

cards.text:
Alguns cogumelos selvagens são deliciosos; outros podem matar. O chapéu-da-morte, Amanita phalloides, causa a maioria das intoxicações fatais por cogumelos, e cresce em Portugal sob carvalhos e outras árvores.

Nenhum teste simples distingue os seguros dos venenosos. Nunca coma um cogumelo selvagem a menos que um especialista o tenha identificado pessoalmente.

quiz.q: O que é um cogumelo?
options: Um corpo de frutificação que espalha esporos
Um tipo de raiz de planta
quiz.explain: O corpo principal do fungo é o micélio, que fica escondido.

quiz.q: O que as plantas dão aos seus fungos micorrízicos?
quiz.explain: Em troca, os fungos trazem água e nutrientes como o fósforo.

quiz.q: Que remédio veio de um bolor do gênero Penicillium?
quiz.explain: Fleming percebeu o seu efeito sobre as bactérias em 1928.

quiz.q: Como saber se um cogumelo selvagem é seguro para comer?
options: Ele deixa uma colher de prata preta
Só pela identificação de um especialista
quiz.explain: Nenhum teste simples funciona, e espécies mortais podem ter uma aparência comum.

cards.title: Em toda parte

items.l: micróbios numa colher de chá de terra

cards.text: Os micróbios, sobretudo bactérias, arqueias, fungos e vírus, vivem em toda parte: no solo, nas nuvens, em fontes termais e dentro de você. Uma colher de chá de terra pode ter bilhões.

deep.x: A **microbe** is any living thing too small to see without a microscope. Most are single cells. They were the first life on Earth, and they still make up most of its diversity.
How small?
A micrometre is a thousandth of a millimetre. About a thousand bacteria lined up would cross the width of a pinhead.
Everywhere means everywhere

x: Soil: a gram can hold up to around a billion bacteria from thousands of species
Air: microbes ride clouds and may help ice crystals form, nudging rain
Deep rock: microbes live kilometres underground
You: your body carries roughly as many bacterial cells as human cells, about 38 trillion, mostly in your gut

deep.w: Microbes are mostly germs
deep.r: Only around 1,400 known microbe species cause human disease, out of millions

deep.x: Microbes are the invisible majority, living in every corner of the planet, including inside you.

cards.title: A primeira vida
cards.text: Durante cerca de 3 bilhões de anos, os micróbios foram a única vida na Terra. As cianobactérias encheram o ar de oxigênio, tornando possível a vida animal.

deep.x: Earth formed about 4.5 billion years ago. Fossil mats of microbes called stromatolites suggest life was present by about 3.5 billion years ago, and possibly earlier. For roughly the next 3 billion years, all life was microscopic.
The oxygen revolution

**Cyanobacteria** were the first organisms to perform the kind of photosynthesis that splits water and releases oxygen. At first, the oxygen reacted with iron dissolved in the sea, rusting out as red layers we can still see in banded iron rocks. Around 2.4 billion years ago, oxygen began to build up in the air: the Great Oxidation Event.

For many early microbes, oxygen was a poison, and many were pushed into oxygen-free corners. But oxygen allowed much more energy to be extracted from food, which eventually made large, active animals possible.
Captured partners
Your cells contain mitochondria, the power stations, which descend from bacteria swallowed by an ancestral cell around 2 billion years ago. Plant chloroplasts are captured cyanobacteria.
Living stromatolites still grow today in a few places, such as Shark Bay in Western Australia, giving a glimpse of early Earth.
Microbes ran the planet alone for about 3 billion years, and their oxygen made animals possible.

cards.title: Bactérias

viz.unit: bactérias a partir de uma célula

cards.text: As bactérias são células únicas sem núcleo. Em boas condições, podem se dividir a cada 20 minutos. A maioria é inofensiva ou útil; algumas causam doenças.

deep.x: A bacterium is a single cell with no nucleus: its DNA floats freely in a loop. Most are 1–5 micrometres long. They have a tough cell wall, and many swim with whip-like tails called flagella.
Shapes
Explosive growth
Bacteria reproduce by splitting in two. In ideal conditions, *E. coli* can divide every 20 minutes.

x: Doubling every 20 min
10 hours = 30 doublings
1 cell becomes over 1 billion

deep.x: In reality, food runs out and waste builds up long before that, which is why fridges, salt and drying preserve food: they slow or stop division.
Mostly friends

x: Gut bacteria break down fibre, make some vitamins (like vitamin K) and train your immune system
Bacteria make yogurt, cheese and vinegar
They recycle nutrients in soil and water
A small minority cause diseases such as tuberculosis, cholera and pneumonia

deep.x: The Dutch cloth merchant Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was the first to see bacteria, in 1676, using a tiny home-made lens. He called them "animalcules".
Bacteria are simple cells that multiply astonishingly fast, and the vast majority keep us and the planet running.

cards.title: Arqueias
cards.text: As arqueias parecem bactérias, mas são um ramo separado da vida. Muitas prosperam em condições extremas: fontes ferventes, lagos salgados e fontes hidrotermais do fundo do mar.

deep.x: Under a microscope, archaea look just like bacteria: small, single cells with no nucleus. But in 1977 the American microbiologist Carl Woese compared their genetic machinery and found they were as different from bacteria as bacteria are from us. Life was split into three great branches.
Lovers of extremes
Their cell membranes are built from unusual fats that stay stable in heat and acid, which helps explain why so many thrive where other cells fall apart.
Not just extremes
Archaea also live in ordinary soils, oceans and your gut. **Methanogens** in cows' stomachs, rice paddies and wetlands produce much of the world's natural methane, a powerful greenhouse gas.
No archaeon is known to cause disease in humans. And their genes suggest that our own branch, the eukaryotes, may have begun when an archaeon merged with a bacterium.
The pinkish-red colour of some salt pans, like those of Aveiro or Castro Marim, comes partly from salt-loving archaea and algae full of red pigments.
Archaea look like bacteria but are a separate branch of life, and they may be our own distant ancestors.

cards.title: Vírus

steps: O vírus se prende à célula

cards.text: Os vírus são minúsculos pacotes de genes que só conseguem se multiplicar dentro de células vivas. Há mais vírus na Terra do que estrelas no universo.

deep.x: A virus is a set of genes, DNA or RNA, wrapped in a protein coat. It has no metabolism of its own: no way to make energy or proteins. To reproduce, it must hijack a living cell. Most are 20–300 nanometres across, far smaller than bacteria.
Alive or not?
Biologists still argue. Viruses evolve and carry genes, but they can't do anything outside a host. Many prefer to call them "at the edge of life".
Numbers beyond imagination
Most viruses infect bacteria, not people. These **bacteriophages** kill a large share of ocean bacteria every day, releasing nutrients that feed the next generation of plankton.

deep.w: Antibiotics can treat viral infections
deep.r: Antibiotics target bacteria; they don't work on viruses like colds or flu

deep.x: Viruses are packets of genes that can only copy themselves inside cells, and they are the most numerous biological entities on Earth.

cards.title: Fermentação
cards.text: Leveduras e bactérias fazem o pão crescer, transformam suco de uva em vinho e leite em iogurte e queijo. Os seres humanos usam a fermentação há milhares de anos.

deep.x: **Fermentation** is how some microbes get energy from sugar without oxygen. It produces leftovers, such as alcohol, carbon dioxide or acids, and humans have learnt to love those leftovers.
sugar (no oxygen) → alcohol + carbon dioxide
How bread rises
Ancient technology

Chemical traces in pottery show fermented drinks in China around 7000 BCE and wine in Georgia around 6000 BCE. People used fermentation for thousands of years without knowing why it worked. In the 1850s and 1860s, Louis Pasteur showed that living microbes were responsible.

items.b: yeast turns grape sugar to alcohol

deep.x: Fermentation also preserves food. Acid and alcohol stop most harmful microbes, which is why sauerkraut, cheese and cured olives keep so well. Portuguese table olives, vinho verde and aged cheeses like Serra da Estrela all depend on microbes.
The sharp, lightly fizzy character of a young vinho verde traditionally comes partly from carbon dioxide left by fermentation.
Fermentation is microbes eating sugar without oxygen, and their leftovers give us bread, wine, cheese and yogurt.

cards.title: Fixadores de nitrogênio
cards.text: As plantas precisam de nitrogênio, mas não conseguem usá-lo direto do ar. Bactérias nas raízes do feijão e da ervilha o convertem numa forma utilizável.

deep.x: Nitrogen is in every protein and every strand of DNA. The air is about 78% nitrogen, but it's locked in N2 molecules held together by a very strong triple bond. Plants and animals can't break it.
A partnership underground

Rhizobium bacteria live inside small lumps, called nodules, on the roots of legumes such as beans, peas, chickpeas, lupins and clover. Using an enzyme called nitrogenase, they turn nitrogen from the air into ammonia the plant can use. In return, the plant gives them sugar. Healthy nodules are pink inside, coloured by a protein that controls oxygen, because oxygen destroys nitrogenase.
Farming with microbes

Farmers have long rotated legumes with cereals to enrich soil, even without knowing why. In the early 1900s, the **Haber–Bosch** process learnt to fix nitrogen industrially, using high heat and pressure to make fertiliser.
Synthetic nitrogen fertiliser grows the food for roughly half the world's population, but excess runs off fields and pollutes rivers and seas.
Bacteria in legume roots do at room temperature what industry needs huge heat and pressure for: pulling nitrogen from the air.

cards.title: Resistência aos antibióticos
cards.text: Quando os antibióticos são usados em excesso, as bactérias resistentes sobrevivem e se multiplicam. As infecções resistentes já causam mais de um milhão de mortes por ano no mundo.

deep.x: Antibiotics kill bacteria or stop them growing. Penicillin, discovered by Alexander Fleming in 1928 and mass-produced from the 1940s, transformed medicine. Fleming himself warned that misuse could make bacteria resistant.
How bacteria resist
Bacteria can also swap resistance genes directly, even between species, on small loops of DNA called plasmids. That means resistance can spread much faster than by inheritance alone.
The scale of the problem

A global study published in 2024 estimated that drug-resistant infections directly caused over a million deaths in 2021, and contributed to several million more. Without action, this is expected to rise by 2050.
Slowing it down

x: Use antibiotics only when a doctor prescribes them, exactly as directed
Reduce routine antibiotic use in farm animals, now banned for growth promotion in the EU
Good hygiene and vaccines prevent infections in the first place
Develop new antibiotics and alternatives such as phage therapy

deep.x: Every unnecessary antibiotic gives resistant bacteria an advantage, so careful use protects everyone's medicines.

cards.title: Decompositores
cards.text: Sem os micróbios, plantas e animais mortos não apodreceriam e os nutrientes não voltariam ao solo. Eles são os recicladores da natureza.

deep.x: When a leaf falls or an animal dies, a crew of bacteria and fungi gets to work. They release enzymes that break tough materials, like cellulose in plant cell walls, into simple molecules they can absorb. What's left goes back to the soil as nutrients.
A team effort
Wood is especially hard to digest because of **lignin**, a tough glue that stiffens cell walls. Only some fungi, called white-rot fungi, can break it down efficiently.
Inside a compost heap
In a well-built compost heap, so much microbial activity happens that the middle can reach 55–65 °C, hot enough to kill many weed seeds and pathogens.
Some scientists think so much coal formed about 300 million years ago partly because fungi that digest lignin had not yet evolved, so dead trees piled up; others dispute this.
Decomposer microbes close the loop of life, turning death and waste back into the nutrients that feed new growth.

cards.title: Micróbios e clima
cards.text: Os micróbios do oceano absorvem carbono e produzem oxigênio; os do solo armazenam ou liberam carbono. O aquecimento pode fazê-los pender para liberar mais.

deep.x: Microbes are major players in the carbon cycle. Some take carbon dioxide out of the air; others put it back. Small changes in their balance can matter for the whole planet.
The ocean's tiny plants

Microscopic phytoplankton, including cyanobacteria and algae, carry out about half of all photosynthesis on Earth. When they die, some sink to the deep sea, carrying carbon with them. This is called the **biological pump**.
The soil's carbon bank
Soils store more carbon than the atmosphere and all plants combined. Microbes decide how long it stays there.
A risky feedback
Frozen Arctic soils, or permafrost, hold huge amounts of old plant material. As they thaw, microbes start eating it, releasing CO2 and methane.
A single ocean cyanobacterium, *Prochlorococcus*, is so abundant that it is thought to be the most numerous photosynthetic organism on Earth.
Microbes can lock carbon away or release it, and warming risks tipping them towards releasing more.

quiz.q: Por quanto tempo os micróbios foram a única vida na Terra?
O que faz o pão crescer?
Por que o uso excessivo de antibióticos é perigoso?
options: Bactérias resistentes sobrevivem e se espalham

cards.title: Extremófilos
cards.text: Os extremófilos são organismos que prosperam em condições que matariam a maior parte da vida: água fervente, ácido, gelo profundo, pressão esmagadora ou radiação alta.

deep.x: The word **extremophile** means "lover of extremes". The term was coined in the 1970s, as scientists kept finding microbes in places once thought sterile. Most extremophiles are single-celled bacteria and archaea, an ancient branch of life that looks like bacteria but works differently inside.
Extreme for whom?

"Extreme" is our point of view. A microbe from a boiling spring can die at 40 °C, the temperature where we feel comfortable. Each extremophile has tuned its proteins, membranes and DNA to its own world.
Iberian extremes

Spain's Río Tinto, in Huelva, runs red and as acidic as lemon juice, around pH 2, because of iron and sulphur from ancient mines. It is still full of microbes, and NASA has used it to practise searching for life on Mars. Closer to home, the pink colour of some salt pans in Aveiro and the Algarve comes from salt-loving microbes.
Champions

x: Deinococcus radiodurans survives about 1,000 times the radiation dose that would kill a person
Microbes live in the Mariana Trench, about 11 km down, at over 1,000 times sea-level pressure
Bacteria have been found living kilometres down in solid rock

deep.w: Extremophiles are rare oddities
deep.r: In the deep crust and oceans they may make up a large share of all microbial life

deep.x: What is deadly for us is simply home for an extremophile.

cards.title: A vida mais quente
cards.text: Algumas arqueias vivem a cerca de 120 °C perto de fontes hidrotermais do fundo do mar, onde a pressão mantém a água líquida. Suas proteínas são feitas para continuar estáveis sob calor extremo.

deep.x: In 1977 the submarine Alvin found hot springs on the seafloor near the Galápagos, surrounded by life. Since then, hundreds of these **hydrothermal vents** have been found, including several on the Mid-Atlantic Ridge near the Azores.

steps: Hot fluid vents, full of minerals

deep.x: Why the water doesn't boil

At 2,500 m depth, the water above presses down with about 250 times the pressure at the surface. Under that weight water stays liquid far above 100 °C. Vent fluid can reach about 400 °C, but microbes live in the cooler edges where hot meets cold.
Built for heat
Heat makes molecules shake apart. Heat-loving archaea fight back:

x: Proteins packed tightly, with extra chemical "staples" holding them together
Cell membranes made of tougher fats that don't melt
Special enzymes that coil DNA more tightly to stop its strands separating

deep.x: The current record is about 122 °C, set in 2008 by Methanopyrus kandleri grown under high pressure in a lab. Many scientists think the upper limit for life is not much higher, perhaps around 150 °C, because key molecules such as ATP fall apart.
Vent microbes don't need sunlight: they get energy from chemicals such as hydrogen sulphide, and feed whole ecosystems of tubeworms, shrimps and crabs.
Pressure keeps vent water liquid, and tough proteins keep life working at temperatures that would cook us.

cards.title: Sobreviver no deserto

items.r: Guardam gordura; o corpo tolera perder água

cards.text: Os camelos podem perder até um quarto do peso do corpo em água e se recuperar bebendo cerca de 100 litros em minutos. As corcovas armazenam gordura, não água.

deep.x: Most mammals are in danger after losing about 15% of their body water; for humans, losses above 10% are serious. A camel can lose around 25% and keep going, then refill fast.

x: 500 kg camel
Loses 25% as water ≈ 125 litres
Drinks about 100 litres in roughly 10 minutes

deep.x: How camels save water

items: Let body heat rise by day

deep.x: A camel's body temperature can swing by about 6 °C, from around 34 °C at dawn to around 40 °C in the afternoon. It stores heat by day instead of sweating it away, and sheds it in the cool night.
Safe drinking
Gulping so much water would burst the blood cells of most animals. Camels' red blood cells are oval and flexible, and can swell to more than twice their size without bursting.
Why the hump?
The hump stores fat, up to tens of kilograms of it. Keeping fat in one place, rather than all over the body, lets heat escape more easily from the rest of the skin.
The kangaroo rat of North American deserts may never drink at all: it gets water from the chemistry of digesting dry seeds.

deep.w: Camels store water in their humps
deep.r: The hump is fat; their real trick is losing very little water and tolerating dehydration

deep.x: Camels survive by spending water slowly, tolerating dehydration and refilling fast.

cards.title: Peixes da Antártida

items: Água gelada e rica em oxigênio

cards.text: Os peixes-gelo têm proteínas anticongelantes no sangue e nenhum glóbulo vermelho, dependendo do oxigênio dissolvido na água gelada.

deep.x: The Southern Ocean around Antarctica is about −1.9 °C. Salt stops seawater from freezing at 0 °C, but the blood of an ordinary fish would freeze at about −0.8 °C. Ice crystals in the water would grow inside it.
Antifreeze in the blood

In the 1960s the American biologist Arthur DeVries found that Antarctic notothenioid fish carry **antifreeze proteins**. They bind to tiny ice crystals and stop them growing. The fish don't stop ice from forming; they stop it from spreading.
Clear-blooded icefish

Icefish, a group of about 16 species, went further. They have no red blood cells and no haemoglobin; their blood is almost colourless. They survive because very cold water holds more dissolved oxygen.

x: A large heart pumping a large volume of blood
Wide blood vessels and many fine capillaries
Skin without scales that can take up some oxygen
A slow, energy-saving lifestyle

deep.x: In 2021 a research ship found an icefish breeding colony under the Weddell Sea covering about 240 km², with an estimated 60 million nests.
Antarctic fish stay liquid with antifreeze, and icefish even manage without red blood.

cards.title: As rãs-da-floresta
cards.text: As rãs-da-floresta do Alasca congelam por inteiro no inverno: o coração para, a respiração para. Na primavera, elas descongelam e saem pulando. O açúcar protege as suas células.

deep.x: Wood frogs live across North America, as far north as Alaska and beyond the Arctic Circle. Instead of digging deep below the frost line, they shelter just under leaf litter and let themselves freeze.
Freezing, carefully

Ice inside a cell tears it apart. So the frog controls where ice forms. Within minutes of the first ice touching its skin, its liver floods the body with glucose. The sugar-rich cells resist freezing and don't shrink too much as water is drawn out. Up to about two-thirds of the frog's body water turns to ice.
Frozen for months

In Alaska, wood frogs have survived temperatures down to about −18 °C and spent up to seven months frozen. Their hearts stop, breathing stops and there is no brain activity. When spring comes they thaw, and within hours the heart restarts.
Lessons for medicine

Donated human organs can be kept outside the body only for hours, because cooling damages them. Researchers study frogs like this one to learn how to store organs longer using natural protective substances.

deep.w: Freezing always kills cells
deep.r: It's ice inside cells that kills; controlling where ice forms makes survival possible

deep.x: A wood frog survives winter by choosing where its ice goes.

cards.title: A vida nas cavernas
cards.text: Os animais de cavernas escuras muitas vezes perdem os olhos e a cor ao longo das gerações e dependem do tato e do olfato. O proteu, uma salamandra das cavernas, pode viver 100 anos.

deep.x: Animals that live their whole lives in caves are called **troglobites**. With no light at all, eyes are useless and colour has no purpose. Over many generations, cave species often lose both, and gain longer antennae, legs or sensory organs instead.
Why lose eyes?

Eyes and the brain areas that run them cost a lot of energy. Caves are poor in food, so animals that waste less energy do better. A study on young fish estimated vision can use around 15% of their resting energy. Mutations that switch off eyes are no longer weeded out, and may even help.
The olm
The olm, or proteus, is a pale, blind salamander about 25 cm long that lives in flooded caves of the Dinaric karst in Slovenia, Croatia and nearby. It keeps feathery gills all its life.
Its metabolism is extremely slow. One olm in a cave in Bosnia was found in the same spot for seven years.
Evolution repeating itself

The Mexican tetra lives in rivers with eyes, and in caves without them. Different cave populations lost their eyes independently, showing the same pressures can produce the same result again and again.
Portugal's limestone caves, such as those of the Serra de Aire e Candeeiros, hold tiny blind invertebrates that live nowhere else.
In permanent darkness, evolution trades eyes and colour for energy savings and sharper touch.

cards.title: Grandes altitudes
cards.text: Os gansos-de-cabeça-listrada voam sobre o Himalaia a cerca de 7,000 m. O sangue deles transporta melhor o oxigênio, e as asas batem com eficiência no ar rarefeito.

deep.x: At 7,000 m the air holds less than half the oxygen per breath that it does at sea level. Most people need bottled oxygen above about 8,000 m. Bar-headed geese cross the Himalayas each year flying under their own power.
What tracking showed

Satellite tags fitted from 2009 onwards showed the geese usually follow passes at around 4,000 to 6,000 m, rising higher only when they must. The highest flight recorded was about 7,300 m. They often fly at night and early morning, when the air is colder and denser, giving more lift and oxygen.
Body upgrades
A single change in the geese's haemoglobin helps it grab oxygen from thin air. Their deep, slow breathing moves more air than ours, and their flight muscles are packed with blood vessels.
People at altitude

Tibetans and Andean highlanders adapted in different ways. Many Tibetans carry a gene variant that stops their blood becoming too thick at altitude; it seems to come from the Denisovans, an extinct human group.
In 1973 a Rüppell's vulture collided with a plane over Ivory Coast at about 11,300 m, the highest bird flight ever recorded.
Bar-headed geese beat thin air with better haemoglobin, bigger breaths and smart timing.

cards.title: Gigantes do fundo do mar
cards.text: No mar profundo e frio, alguns animais ficam enormes, como a lula-gigante, com até cerca de 12 m, e os isópodes-gigantes. O frio e o metabolismo lento permitem corpos maiores.

deep.x: Some deep-sea animals are much bigger than their shallow-water relatives. This is called **deep-sea gigantism**. Biologists see a similar pattern in cold polar waters, so temperature seems to matter.
Why bigger?

In cold water, metabolism runs slowly, so animals grow slowly but keep growing for longer. Large bodies also use less energy per kilogram and can travel far between scarce meals. Cold water holds more oxygen, helping big bodies breathe.
The giants

x: **Giant squid**: females reach about 12 m including the long tentacles, with eyes the size of dinner plates. It was first filmed alive in the deep in 2012, off Japan.
**Colossal squid**: shorter but heavier, up to about 500 kg. A young one was first filmed in the wild in 2025.
**Giant isopod**: a woodlouse relative up to about 50 cm long. One in a Japanese aquarium refused food for over five years.

deep.x: Iberian connections

Giant squid are sometimes found stranded or caught off Portugal and northern Spain, where deep canyons come close to shore. Luarca, in Asturias, has a museum devoted to them. In Madeira, fishermen catch black scabbardfish at around 1,000 m deep.

deep.w: Deep-sea giants are monsters that attack ships
deep.r: They are slow, rarely seen animals that avoid the surface

deep.x: Cold, slow lives let some deep-sea animals keep growing into giants.

cards.title: Sobreviventes do espaço
cards.text: Tardígrados e algumas bactérias sobreviveram à exposição ao espaço sideral em satélites. Os líquens também.

deep.x: Space is a near-perfect vacuum, bathed in harsh ultraviolet and cosmic radiation, with temperatures swinging hundreds of degrees. Yet a few organisms have survived being left outside spacecraft.
Tardigrades

Tardigrades, or water bears, are animals about half a millimetre long, with eight stubby legs. You can find them in moss on a Portuguese wall. When dry, they curl into a **tun**, losing most of their water and almost stopping their metabolism.

In 2007, on the European Space Agency's TARDIS experiment, dried tardigrades spent 10 days exposed in orbit. Many survived vacuum and cosmic rays; most, but not all, died when also exposed to full solar ultraviolet.
Protecting the DNA

Tardigrades make a sugar called trehalose that turns into a glass-like solid, holding cell parts in place. In 2016 scientists found a protein, called Dsup, that partly shields their DNA from radiation.
Lichens and bacteria

Lichens, partnerships of fungus and alga, survived 15 days in open space in 2005 and later longer stays outside the ISS. Clumps of the bacterium Deinococcus survived three years outside the ISS, in a Japanese experiment.

deep.w: Tardigrades are indestructible
deep.r: They survive by shutting down; in an active state they are fragile, and many die in space tests

deep.x: Some life can wait out space by drying up and switching off.

cards.title: Por que isso importa
cards.text: Os extremófilos nos ajudam a imaginar a vida em outros mundos e nos dão ferramentas úteis: uma enzima de uma bactéria de fontes termais é a base dos testes de PCR usados na medicina.

deep.x: In the 1960s the American microbiologist Thomas Brock found a bacterium, Thermus aquaticus, in the hot springs of Yellowstone. Its enzyme for copying DNA, called **Taq polymerase**, keeps working after being heated near boiling. That made it perfect for PCR, the DNA-copying method invented by Kary Mullis in 1983.

x: Each cycle doubles the DNA
After 30 cycles: 2^30
About 1 billion copies from one

deep.x: PCR is used for COVID-19 tests, forensic DNA, diagnosing infections and checking food. Without a heat-proof enzyme, fresh enzyme would have to be added after every heating step.
Other useful tricks
Life beyond Earth

If microbes live in boiling acid, ice and rock on Earth, life elsewhere seems more plausible. Mars may have salty water underground. Jupiter's moon Europa and Saturn's moon Enceladus hide oceans beneath their ice. Europe's JUICE probe, launched in 2023, and NASA's Europa Clipper, launched in 2024, will study these icy moons in the early 2030s.
Spain's acidic Río Tinto has been used to test equipment designed to look for life on Mars.
A microbe from a hot spring gave us PCR, and extremophiles tell us where to look for life beyond Earth.
